label: policy, numbers
q: What has Canada's national pharmacare program actually delivered since the Pharmacare Act passed in 2024: which provinces and territories have signed agreements, what is covered, how many people are using it, and what do the Parliamentary Budget Officer and other independent estimates say the full program would cost?

report.title: What Canada's Pharmacare Act Has Actually Delivered: Agreements, Coverage, Uptake, and What Full Pharmacare Would Cost

review.sentence: As of 26 January 2026, agreements were in force with four jurisdictions: > "The Government of Canada has signed funding agreements with four provinces and territories to make a range of contraception and diabetes medications free." [1] Residents of the other nine provinces and territories have no access to the program at all, whatever their eligibility would be.
review.why: The support checker gives about 11% that the passages noted from [1] state this.

sentences.sentence: Section 6(1) does not create a national drug plan; it creates a conditional spending power: > "**6** (1) The Minister must, if the Minister has entered into an agreement with a province or territory to do so, make payments to the province or territory in order to increase any existing public pharmacare coverage — and to provide universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage — for specific prescription drugs and related products intended for contraception or the treatment of diabetes." [5] Three features of that drafting determine everything that follows.

Section 11(1) required the Minister to establish a committee of experts within 30 days of royal assent: > "**11** (1) The Minister must, no later than 30 days after the day on which this Act receives royal assent, establish a committee of experts, and provide for its membership, to make recommendations respecting options for the operation and financing of national, universal, single-payer pharmacare." [5] Beyond that committee, the Act directs Canada's Drug Agency to develop a list of essential drugs and related products to inform a national formulary, a national bulk purchasing strategy, and a pan-Canadian strategy on appropriate prescribing, and it establishes a fund for diabetes devices and supplies [8].

Writing in the Canadian Medical Association Journal, health law and policy scholars made the point directly: > "However, Bill C-64 does not establish the CDA by law, nor set out the agency’s powers, functions, and governance structures, which represents a missed opportunity to depoliticize the implementation and management of national pharmacare." [9] That matters for the question of what has been delivered, because the agency that must produce the formulary the whole architecture depends on exists by federal announcement and budget appropriation, not by statute, and so is exposed to exactly the political direction the Act's proponents wanted to insulate it from. *Inference:* the Act is best read as a funding framework for a first phase plus a set of study and strategy obligations, not as the legal foundation of universal pharmacare.

The page states plainly: > "The Government of Canada has signed funding agreements with four provinces and territories to make a range of contraception and diabetes medications free." [1] That is four of thirteen provinces and territories.

The federal contribution is more than $219 million over four years: > "Through this first-ever national pharmacare agreement, the Government of Canada will provide more than $219 million over four years for universal coverage to a range of contraceptives and diabetes medications for Manitobans." [3] The announcement anticipated coverage for the majority of products from June 2025 [3], but the agreement itself fixes the Implementation Date at 15 April 2025 [16] — earlier than announced.
Manitoba also agreed to provide free hormone replacement therapy, an add-on beyond the federal contraception-and-diabetes template [15].

The agreement's own figures are $52,509,230 in Stream 1 funding for 2025-26 and $54,603,615 in each of the next three years, plus a one-time $9,945,348 for diabetes devices in 2025-26 [16]. **British Columbia** signed 6 March 2025, the largest of the four deals: > "Today, the Honourable Mark Holland, Canada's Minister of Health, and the Honourable Josie Osborne, British Columbia's (BC) Minister of Health, announced the signing of a pharmacare agreement to invest more than $670 million over four years to provide universal access to contraceptive and diabetes medications, devices and supplies for residents of BC." [2] The agreement text gives the exact federal allocations and shows how the money is back-loaded: $17,406,567 in fiscal 2025-26, then $204,948,289 in each of 2026-27, 2027-28 and 2028-29, plus a one-time $37,839,549 for diabetes devices in 2026-27 [6].
Adding those stated instalments gives roughly $670 million — my own arithmetic from the agreement's schedule, and it matches the "more than $670 million" in the news release [2].

BC's agreement also writes a provincial add-on into the federal terms: > "Effective on March 1, 2026, British Columbia will provide free public coverage of hormone replacement therapies identified by British Columbia to treat menopausal symptoms for all Residents." [6] **Prince Edward Island** signed in March 2025.

The pharmacare component is more than $30 million over four years, part of a $40 million two-agreement package that also covers rare diseases: > "Through the national pharmacare agreement, the Government of Canada will provide more than $30 million over four years for universal coverage to a range of contraceptives and diabetes medications for PEI residents, at little to no direct cost to them." [4] PEI's coverage began 1 May 2025 — the earliest actual start date of the four. **Yukon** signed 20 March 2025, the smallest deal: > "announced the signing of a pharmacare agreement to invest up to $9.5 million over four years to provide universal access to contraceptive and diabetes medications for residents of Yukon." [7] Yukon's coverage was to begin no later than January 2026 [7].
Manitoba's binding Implementation Date is 15 April 2025 [16], PEI's coverage began 1 May 2025 [4], Yukon's no later than January 2026 [7], and BC's on 1 March 2026 [6].

The second is that the federal template is being amended at the provincial level: both Manitoba and BC extracted free hormone replacement therapy as a condition of signing [6][15], which is outside the Act's contraception-and-diabetes scope. *Inference:* that is a sign of provinces using their leverage in a voluntary, agreement-by-agreement structure, and it means "what pharmacare covers" already differs by province before universal pharmacare has been legislated at all.

Health Canada's February 2024 backgrounder on contraception set out the list: > "This includes oral contraceptives, copper and hormonal IUDs, injections, implants, rings, and morning-after pills." [10] The accompanying diabetes announcement defined the other half of the basket as first-line glucose-lowering treatment: > "Today’s announcement would ensure that, following agreement with PTs, diabetics in Canada will have access to first-line treatments for diabetes that lower blood glucose levels, including:" [11] The items that follow that colon in the government's own document are insulin, metformin, sulfonylureas and SGLT-2 inhibitors, with specific brand and generic products named.

Alongside the drugs sits a separate fund for diabetes devices and supplies — test strips, lancets, insulin pumps and advanced glucose monitors — which is why BC's agreement carries a distinct one-time $37,839,549 allocation for devices in 2026-27 [6]. **The actual coverage list is longer and more conditional than "first-line treatments" suggests.** The Manitoba agreement's Annex A is the operative legal list for that province, and it includes long-acting insulin degludec, the SGLT-2 inhibitors dapagliflozin, empagliflozin and canagliflozin, several DPP-4 inhibitors, and the GLP-1 combination lixisenatide with insulin glargine [16].

But most of the newer agents are listed as Exception Drug Status benefits, available only in exceptional circumstances with prior approval from Manitoba, while the open benefits are the older, cheaper products — the insulins, metformin, glyburide and gliclazide [16].

So the basket is not narrow in the sense of excluding modern drugs; it is narrow in the sense that modern drugs sit behind a prior-approval gate that older drugs do not. **Some products are capped.** Emergency contraception is listed as an open benefit but with a hard limit: a "Maximum of 3 treatments (3 tablets) per benefit year" [16].

In practice Manitoba's program also caps the professional fee it will cover at $14, limited to once a month for diabetes medications and once every three months for oral contraceptives [15]. **Two exclusions matter more than the inclusions.** First, Ozempic (semaglutide) is not covered at no cost in Manitoba, and the province gives the reason plainly: "Ozempic was not included in the federal list of medications for no-cost coverage for discussion with provinces and territories." [15] The basket is federal, and it overrides clinical practice — semaglutide is widely prescribed for diabetes in Canada, and its absence is a direct consequence of the federal list, not a Manitoba judgement.

Manitoba states that "Diabetes supplies remain as benefits under the Manitoba Pharmacare Program (where deductibles apply), and other provincial programs such as Employment and Income Assistance." [15] So the device half of the program, funded by a separate one-time federal payment, had not by 2026 delivered no-cost supplies in at least one of the four provinces; it expanded eligibility for pumps and monitors that were already covered subject to deductibles. **Provinces are adding to the federal basket, not just implementing it.** Manitoba's program covers four categories — birth control, diabetes, HIV prevention and treatment, and hormone replacement therapy — but only two are federally funded: "Federal funding for National Pharmacare has been provided to Manitoba in support of no cost coverage of diabetes and birth control medications." [15] HIV medications and HRT are provincial additions.

BC's agreement likewise obliges it to cover hormone replacement therapies from 1 March 2026 [6]. *Inference:* the voluntary, agreement-by-agreement structure gives provinces leverage to extract a broader provincial basket, so "what pharmacare covers" already varies by jurisdiction before any national formulary exists. **On whether federal money substitutes for provincial spending**, the agreements are more careful than the public debate assumes.
Manitoba's contains an explicit anti-substitution clause: if the province's own Stream 1 spending falls below its 2022-23 baseline, Canada withholds an equivalent amount [16].
The baseline is published in the agreement — Manitoba spent $23,945,982 on the Annex A drugs in 2022-23, of which just $750,746 was contraception [16].
Against that, the federal Stream 1 allocation is $52,509,230 in 2025-26 rising to $54,603,615 [16].

That is not a reporting failure that a better search would fix; it follows from how the program is built, and the design is documented. **There is no enrolment.** Manitoba's program page describes the entire process: "Present the prescription for an eligible MEPP product and your Manitoba Health card at a pharmacy." [15] The pharmacist checks whether the person has 100 per cent coverage elsewhere, then processes the claim.
Eligibility is having an active Manitoba Health card and not already being covered by a federal or another provincial plan [15].

Because there is no enrolment step, there is no register to count, and the only possible measure of use is claims data held by the province and its pharmacy network. **The agreements do not require a headcount.** Manitoba's funding agreement obliges it, from fiscal 2026-27, to submit an attested financial statement showing how much federal money was received and spent on product costs [16], and to report the dollar value of "Savings" delivered on diabetes devices [16].

The federal government is therefore not collecting the number the question asks for, by design. **What can be established is the ceiling on who could possibly use it.** As of the Health Canada page's last update on 26 January 2026, four jurisdictions had agreements [1], and residents of the other nine had no access at all.

Within the four, coverage start dates are set in the agreements and staggered: Manitoba's Implementation Date is fixed at 15 April 2025 [16]; PEI's coverage began 1 May 2025 [4]; Yukon's no later than January 2026 [7]; BC's on 1 March 2026 [6].

Manitoba's start came earlier than the federal news release anticipated — the release said coverage was anticipated from June 2025 [3], while the binding agreement specifies 15 April 2025 [16] — which is a useful reminder that the agreement text, not the announcement, governs. **The government's planning figures give intended scale, not measured use.** For BC: 1.3 million people for contraception and nearly 550,000 with diabetes [2].
For PEI: more than 41,000 for contraception and 16,000 with diabetes [4].
For Yukon: more than 12,000 and over 3,000 [7].

Summing the diabetes figures for BC, PEI and Yukon — Manitoba's release gives no comparable count [3] — gives a little over half a million people, against Health Canada's national figure that "About 3.8 million people in Canada have been diagnosed with diabetes" [12].

That arithmetic is mine, not a government statement. **A published baseline lets the fiscal question be answered even without a headcount.** Manitoba's Annex B discloses that the province spent $23,945,982 in 2022-23 on the drugs now in Annex A — $23,195,236 on diabetes and $750,746 on contraception — plus $1,449,593 on insulin pumps and advanced glucose monitors [16].
Those are the amounts a public plan paid, excluding patient copays and deductibles [16].

Since federal Stream 1 funding is $52,509,230 in 2025-26 [16], Ottawa is now paying roughly twice what Manitoba's public plan spent on the same products three years earlier, which is consistent with the program reaching people who were previously paying out of pocket rather than merely re-insuring the province.

Manitoba's own materials point to the gap: free birth control without a health card is available only through community health clinics and teen clinics [15], and a prescription is still required for emergency contraception — if the patient has none, a pharmacist may write one but may charge a fee that the program does not cover [15]. *Inference:* the population most likely to benefit — young people and people without a regular primary care provider — faces the highest non-price barriers, so early claims volumes will understate unmet need, and the absence of any published claims series makes the size of that gap unmeasurable from public sources.

Its central finding: > "Upon the implementation of a single-payer universal drug plan based on Quebec’s Régie de l’assurance maladie du Québec (RAMQ) formulary— “Pharmacare”—we estimate the incremental cost to the public sector (that is federal and provincial governments combined) to be $11.2 billion in 2024-25, increasing to $13.4 billion in 2027-28." [14] **The PBO refuses to give a federal number, and says why.** This is the single most important caveat in the whole literature, and it is routinely ignored by people who attribute an "$11.2 billion federal cost" to the PBO: > "As there is no certainty with respect to the federal and provincial shares of the cost of such a program, it is not possible to isolate federal costs." [14] The $11.2 billion is a combined federal-plus-provincial figure.

There is no PBO estimate of what Ottawa alone would pay, because that depends on a cost-sharing model no government has chosen. **Gross and net differ by about $3.6 billion.** The PBO's own decomposition: total drug expenditure under pharmacare of $33.2 billion in 2024-25 rising to $38.9 billion in 2027-28; a gross cost incremental to existing public drug plans of $14.8 billion rising to $17.3 billion; and a net incremental public cost of $11.2 billion rising to $13.4 billion after crediting savings on direct federal spending and pharmacare copayment revenues [14].

So the gross incremental cost is "the cost of pharmacare" in one sense and the net is the cost in another, and the two differ by roughly a third. **The PBO costed three different baskets, and the results differ by nearly an order of magnitude.** This is the answer to why published estimates disagree so wildly: - **RAMQ formulary** (the full Quebec list, universal, with a $5 brand-name copay and exemptions): incremental public cost of $11.2 billion in 2024-25, $13.4 billion in 2027-28 [14]. - **Catastrophic formulary** (only drugs that could cause undue financial hardship, drawn from the catastrophic programs of BC, Ontario, Newfoundland and Labrador and PEI): incremental public cost of $1.8 billion in 2024-25 and $2.0 billion in 2027-28 [14]. - **Essential medicines formulary** (the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines adapted for Canada by researchers at St.
Michael's Hospital in Toronto): drug expenditures of $0.4 billion and $0.3 billion *more* than the baseline in 2024-25 and 2027-28 [14].

The PBO's explanation is that the list "consists primarily of generic drugs, the prices for which are already sufficiently low that little additional savings can be achieved with a single-payer plan." The higher expenditures are therefore the result of increased drug use that is not offset by negotiating savings [14]. **The National Pharmacare Committee of Experts adopted the PBO as its ceiling and produced a lower floor.** The committee, created under section 11 of the Act, reported in 2025 with a range: > "The total cost of publicly funding a list of essential medicines will likely be between $6 to $10 billion dollars (see Appendix 2)." [13] Its upper bound is explicitly the PBO's work: "We used the 2023 report from the Parliamentary Budget Office to estimate the upper bound of the cost of pharmacare." [13] Its lower bound is its own bottom-up model.

It took the 185 essential medicines with multiple sources and no patent protection — the set the pan-Canadian Pharmaceutical Alliance identified as tendering candidates — and found that "In 2024, total spending on these 185 medicines was $12.6 billion." [13] It then applied generic pricing (−14%), lower public-plan markups (−17%) and competitive tendering (−40%) to reach $6.0 billion.

The committee's −40% tendering assumption is also contingent on a policy change not yet made — it notes that the pCPA's agreement to avoid competitive tendering expires in 2026 [13]. **On the savings side**, the committee estimates "direct savings of up to $18 billion to all public drug plans" [13], plus indirect savings from reduced hospitalisations "estimated to be larger than $1,000 per person per year for those currently unable to afford medicines" [13].

The $18 billion figure covers a far broader basket than the $6–10 billion cost estimate, so the two cannot be netted against each other; the $1,000 figure is a benefit estimate, not a fiscal offset, and is given without a source population or uncertainty range. **Scale, for judging all of the above.** The committee reports that prescription drug spending from all payers rose from $34 billion in 2019 to $44 billion in 2024 [13], and puts the 2024 figure at about $45 billion, equal to roughly 11% of the federal budget: > "The approximate $45 billion spent on prescription medicines (from all payers) in 2024 in Canada is similar to the amount spent on post-secondary education and more than the total budgets of Indigenous Services Canada, Health Canada, Veterans Affairs, the Department of Industry and the Mortgage and Housing Corporation combined." [13] A $6–10 billion gross federal cost is therefore between roughly a seventh and a quarter of all-payer drug spending — large enough to be a genuine reallocation, and far short of absorbing the whole drug bill.

Same model, same data, same behavioural assumptions; changing only the formulary produces an incremental public cost of $1.8 billion (catastrophic), $11.2 billion (RAMQ) or roughly zero to negative (essential medicines) [14].

Gross versus net.** The PBO's RAMQ scenario has a gross incremental cost of $14.8 billion and a net incremental public cost of $11.2 billion in the same year, the difference being savings on direct federal spending and copayment revenues [14].
Whether the behavioural effect is counted.** The PBO assumes that cutting patient-borne prices by 47% to 100% raises prescription utilization by 13.5% [14].
It is also the mechanism that explains why the essential medicines list costs *more* than baseline despite being made of cheap generics [14]. **4.

What counts as a saving.** The PBO's economy-wide savings are modest and specific: $1.4 billion in 2024-25 rising to $2.2 billion in 2027-28, because pharmacare's expenditure growth of 5.3% is slower than the 5.8% baseline, as private plans historically grow faster than public ones [14].
The committee's "$1,000 per person per year" [13] is a health-benefit estimate, not a resource saving, and the two get conflated constantly. **5.

The federal share, which nobody has costed.** Because the PBO declines to isolate federal costs [14], every claim about what Ottawa would spend on full pharmacare is an assumption about a cost-sharing formula, not an estimate. **Why the public cost rises at all is worth stating plainly.** In 2021-22, of $36.6 billion in non-hospital prescription drug spending, 46% ($16.9 billion) was paid by public sources, 40% ($14.7 billion) by private insurance and 14% ($4.9 billion) out of pocket [14].

Manitoba's Stream 1 allocation is $52,509,230 in 2025-26 rising to $54,603,615 in each of the following three years, plus a one-time $9,945,348 for diabetes devices [16]; its agreement began paying in June 2025, with half the first year's amount on signing and the balance in November [16].
BC receives $17,406,567 in 2025-26 against $204,948,289 in each of 2026-27 to 2028-29, plus $37,839,549 for devices [6] — because its implementation date is 1 March 2026 [6].

Adding the four published agreement values gives just under a billion dollars over four years: more than $670 million for BC [2], more than $219 million for Manitoba [3], more than $30 million for PEI [4] and up to $9.5 million for Yukon [7].

Second, the scale is not comparable to the full-program estimates: under a billion dollars over four years for two therapeutic areas in four jurisdictions, against $6–10 billion a year gross for an essential medicines program covering 185 medicines, or $11.2–13.4 billion a year incremental public cost for a RAMQ-style plan [13][14].

The first phase is roughly two orders of magnitude below the full program in annual terms. **For proportion, the committee's own comparison:** > "The federal government has recently announced several new policies that advance national priorities related to equity including a dental care program and a childcare program (with annual costs estimated at $4.4 billion and $7.7 billion, respectively)." [13] On the committee's range, full pharmacare sits between those two.

It also identified plausible funding sources, noting that the exemption of employer contributions to private drug plans from income tax is worth about $5 billion a year and the exemption of prescription medicines from sales tax about $1.1 billion [13] — together covering the low end of its range.

notes.quote: The Government of Canada has signed funding agreements with four provinces and territories to make a range of contraception and diabetes medications free.
notes.claim: As of Health Canada's page (updated 2026-01-26), only four jurisdictions — British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island and Yukon — have signed national pharmacare bilateral agreements, out of 13 provinces and territories.

notes.quote: Today, the Honourable Mark Holland, Canada's Minister of Health, and the Honourable Josie Osborne, British Columbia's (BC) Minister of Health, announced the signing of a pharmacare agreement to invest more than $670 million over four years to provide universal access to contraceptive and diabetes medications, devices and supplies for residents of BC.
notes.claim: British Columbia's agreement, signed March 6, 2025, is worth more than $670 million over four years, covering an estimated 1.3 million people for contraception and nearly 550,000 people with diabetes; BC also added free hormone replacement therapy as a condition of the deal, with coverage starting March 2026.

notes.quote: Through this first-ever national pharmacare agreement, the Government of Canada will provide more than $219 million over four years for universal coverage to a range of contraceptives and diabetes medications for Manitobans.
notes.claim: Manitoba's agreement, announced February 27, 2025, was the first national pharmacare deal: more than $219 million over four years, with coverage anticipated for the majority of products from June 2025; Manitoba also agreed to provide free hormone replacement therapy.

notes.quote: Through the national pharmacare agreement, the Government of Canada will provide more than $30 million over four years for universal coverage to a range of contraceptives and diabetes medications for PEI residents, at little to no direct cost to them.
notes.claim: PEI's agreement provides more than $30 million over four years for pharmacare (part of a $40 million two-agreement package including rare diseases), covering over 41,000 Islanders for contraception and 16,000 with diabetes, with coverage starting May 1, 2025.

notes.quote: **6** (1) The Minister must, if the Minister has entered into an agreement with a province or territory to do so, make payments to the province or territory in order to increase any existing public pharmacare coverage — and to provide universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage — for specific prescription drugs and related products intended for contraception or the treatment of diabetes.
notes.claim: The Pharmacare Act (S.C. 2024, c. 24, assented to 10 October 2024) only obliges the Minister to pay provinces/territories where an agreement exists; coverage is limited in law to contraception and diabetes products, and the payment is conditional on first-dollar coverage.

notes.quote: **11** (1) The Minister must, no later than 30 days after the day on which this Act receives royal assent, establish a committee of experts, and provide for its membership, to make recommendations respecting options for the operation and financing of national, universal, single-payer pharmacare.
notes.claim: The Act creates a statutory committee of experts (to be appointed within 30 days, report within one year and tabled in Parliament) to recommend options for operating and financing universal single-payer pharmacare.

notes.quote: The maximum amounts to be transferred to British Columbia over 4 years are: $17,406,567 in Fiscal Year 2025-26 $204,948,289 in Fiscal Year 2026-27 $204,948,289 in Fiscal Year 2027-28 $204,948,289 in Fiscal Year 2028-29
notes.claim: The BC agreement's exact federal allocations: Stream 1 totals $632,251,434 over four fiscal years ($17,406,567 in 2025-26, then $204,948,289 annually for 2026-27 to 2028-29) plus a one-time $37,839,549 for diabetes devices in 2026-27 — about $670 million, matching the news release.

notes.quote: Effective on March 1, 2026, British Columbia will provide free public coverage of hormone replacement therapies identified by British Columbia to treat menopausal symptoms for all Residents.
notes.claim: The BC agreement sets BC's implementation date for first-dollar contraception and diabetes coverage at March 1, 2026, and requires BC to provide free public coverage of hormone replacement therapy for menopausal symptoms from that date — a provincial add-on written into the deal.

notes.quote: announced the signing of a pharmacare agreement to invest up to $9.5 million over four years to provide universal access to contraceptive and diabetes medications for residents of Yukon.
notes.claim: Yukon's agreement, signed March 20, 2025, is worth up to $9.5 million over four years — the smallest of the four deals — covering contraception and diabetes medications and devices for Yukon residents.

notes.quote: Yukon residents can anticipate beginning to receive coverage for these products no later than January 2026.
notes.claim: Yukon's coverage was to begin no later than January 2026; Yukon's release estimated more than 12,000 Yukoners would gain contraceptive coverage and over 3,000 residents with diabetes.

notes.quote: The Act also requires that Canada’s Drug Agency develop a list of essential drugs and related products to inform the development of a national formulary, a national bulk purchasing strategy to help further reduce drug prices, and a pan-Canadian strategy on the appropriate use of prescription medications.
notes.claim: Government's own summary of the Act's institutional obligations: Canada's Drug Agency to produce an essential drugs list for a national formulary, a national bulk purchasing strategy, a pan-Canadian appropriate-use strategy, and a committee of experts within 30 days; plus a fund for diabetes devices and supplies.

notes.quote: However, Bill C-64 does not establish the CDA by law, nor set out the agency’s powers, functions, and governance structures, which represents a missed opportunity to depoliticize the implementation and management of national pharmacare.
notes.claim: The Act does not itself establish the Canadian Drug Agency in law or define its powers, functions and governance — a key institutional gap identified by health law/policy scholars.

notes.quote: This includes oral contraceptives, copper and hormonal IUDs, injections, implants, rings, and morning-after pills.
notes.claim: Health Canada's Feb 2024 backgrounder defines the contraception basket: oral pills, copper and hormonal IUDs, injections (Depo-Provera), implants (Nexplanon), rings (Haloette) and emergency contraception — a named list of specific products, not a class-based open formulary.

notes.quote: Today’s announcement would ensure that, following agreement with PTs, diabetics in Canada will have access to first-line treatments for diabetes that lower blood glucose levels, including:
notes.claim: Health Canada framed the diabetes basket explicitly as "first-line treatments" that lower blood glucose — insulin, metformin, sulfonylureas and SGLT-2 inhibitors — with named brand/generic products attached to the backgrounder.

notes.quote: The Government of Canada has signed funding agreements with four provinces and territories to make a range of contraception and diabetes medications free.
notes.claim: As of the page's last update (2026-01-26), only four jurisdictions — British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island and Yukon — have pharmacare funding agreements in force, so the pool of people who can use the program at all is limited to those four jurisdictions' residents.

notes.quote: About 3.8 million people in Canada have been diagnosed with diabetes.
notes.claim: Health Canada's own figure for the potential diabetes population is 3.8 million diagnosed people nationally — the denominator against which any take-up of the diabetes half of pharmacare would be judged.

notes.quote: The total cost of publicly funding a list of essential medicines will likely be between $6 to $10 billion dollars (see Appendix 2).
notes.claim: The National Pharmacare Committee of Experts (created by the Pharmacare Act, reported 2025) estimates the gross cost of publicly funding an essential medicines list at $6–10 billion a year — far below the 2019 Advisory Council's $15.3 billion figure.

notes.quote: Total spending on prescribed drugs in Canada jumped by $10 billion in 5 years – from $34 billion in 2019 to $44 billion in 2024
notes.claim: Baseline context: total Canadian spending on prescribed drugs rose from $34B (2019) to $44B (2024), per the Committee of Experts citing CIHI-type data.

notes.quote: In 2024, total spending on these 185 medicines was $12.6 billion.
notes.claim: The Committee's lower bound comes from IQVIA CompuScript dispensing data: 185 essential medicines with multiple sources and no patent protection (identified by pCPA as tendering candidates) cost $12.6 billion in 2024, adjusted to $6.0 billion after assuming generic pricing (−14%), lower public-plan markups (−17%) and competitive pricing (−40%).

notes.quote: We used the 2023 report from the Parliamentary Budget Office to estimate the upper bound of the cost of pharmacare.
notes.claim: The Committee's upper bound is built directly on the PBO's 2023 costing: a longer Quebec RAMQ-style list would cost $35 billion in total in 2025-26 with $11.9 billion incremental to the public sector, while a shorter essential medicines list was estimated at $9.8 billion — the figure the Committee adopts as its ceiling.

notes.quote: First dollar coverage for certain classes of beneficiaries varies from jurisdiction to jurisdiction, but there will be direct savings of up to $18 billion to all public drug plans.
notes.claim: The Committee estimates that full first-dollar federal pharmacare would produce direct savings of up to $18 billion for existing public drug plans (because pharmacare would displace what provinces already pay), plus indirect savings from reduced hospitalizations — which is why the gross and net federal cost differ so much.

notes.quote: The approximate $45 billion spent on prescription medicines (from all payers) in 2024 in Canada is similar to the amount spent on post-secondary education and more than the total budgets of Indigenous Services Canada, Health Canada, Veterans Affairs, the Department of Industry and the Mortgage and Housing Corporation combined.
notes.claim: Scale context for the cost question: about $45 billion was spent on prescription medicines from all payers in Canada in 2024, equal to roughly 11% of the federal budget and more than the combined budgets of several federal departments.

notes.quote: The federal government has recently announced several new policies that advance national priorities related to equity including a dental care program and a childcare program (with annual costs estimated at $4.4 billion and $7.7 billion, respectively).
notes.claim: The Committee explicitly compares pharmacare's cost to other new federal programs: dental care at $4.4 billion a year and childcare at $7.7 billion a year, neither with a dedicated revenue source — establishing that a $6–10B gross pharmacare cost is of the same order as programs already operating.

notes.quote: Reductions in tax revenue due to tax code exemptions relevant to medicine access include the exemption of employer contributions to privately administered insurance plans from income tax ($5 billion annually) and the exemption of prescription medicines from sales tax for consumers ($1.1 billion annually).
notes.claim: The Committee identifies the tax expenditures that could fund pharmacare, including the $5 billion annual exemption of employer contributions to private drug plans and $1.1 billion exemption of prescription medicines from sales tax — and notes private drug insurance collected $61 billion in premiums in 2023, paying $48 billion in claims with medicines at $15 billion (32%).

notes.quote: We assume that the federal government will cover the entire cost of covered medicines, and that the contribution from provincial and territorial governments will be zero. This is unlike the bilateral agreements for diabetes treatments and contraceptives, where there is cost sharing and the federal government covers only the anticipated incremental cost.
notes.claim: The committee's published appendix explicitly explains why phase-one federal payments are far below its full-program estimate: the $6-10B assumes the federal government pays 100% of drug costs, whereas the bilateral agreements fund only the anticipated incremental cost. So a published document does reconcile the two figures.

notes.quote: Upon the implementation of a single-payer universal drug plan based on Quebec’s Régie de l’assurance maladie du Québec (RAMQ) formulary— “Pharmacare”—we estimate the incremental cost to the public sector (that is federal and provincial governments combined) to be $11.2 billion in 2024-25, increasing to $13.4 billion in 2027-28.
notes.claim: PBO's headline finding: a single-payer universal drug plan on the RAMQ formulary would cost the public sector (federal and provincial combined) an incremental $11.2 billion in 2024-25, rising to $13.4 billion in 2027-28.

notes.quote: As there is no certainty with respect to the federal and provincial shares of the cost of such a program, it is not possible to isolate federal costs.
notes.claim: PBO states it cannot isolate the federal share of pharmacare cost, because the federal/provincial split depends on a cost-sharing model not yet chosen — directly relevant to any claim about what Ottawa would pay.

notes.quote: PBO estimates the gross cost incremental to that of public drug plans will be $14.8 billion in 2024-25, increasing to $17.3 billion in 2027-28.
notes.claim: PBO's gross and net figures for the RAMQ-formulary plan: total drug expenditure under pharmacare $33.2B in 2024-25 rising to $38.9B in 2027-28; gross cost incremental to public drug plans $14.8B rising to $17.3B; net incremental public cost $11.2B rising to $13.4B after savings on direct federal spending and copayment revenue.

notes.quote: PBO estimates that drug expenditures under this alternative to be $0.4 billion and $0.3 billion more than the estimated spending under the baseline scenario in 2024-25 and 2027-28 respectively.
notes.claim: PBO's essential medicines alternative — the basket the Committee of Experts built on — actually costs slightly MORE than baseline ($0.4B in 2024-25, $0.3B in 2027-28), because these are already-cheap generics so there are few savings, and increased use from lower copays outweighs them. This is a crucial counterweight to claims that an essential medicines list saves money.

notes.quote: the incremental cost of a single-payer universal drug plan with a catastrophic formulary to the public sector (that is, federal and provincial governments combined) is $1.8 billion and $2.0 billion in 2024-25 and 2027-28 respectively.
notes.claim: PBO estimates a catastrophic-formulary plan would cost the public sector only $1.8B in 2024-25 rising to $2.0B in 2027-28 — a third distinct basket, an order of magnitude below the RAMQ plan.

notes.quote: Prices borne directly by patients are expected to fall by 47 per cent to 100 per cent, which results in overall increases in the utilization of prescription drugs of 13.5 per cent.
notes.claim: PBO assumes reducing patient-borne prices by 47-100% would increase prescription utilization by 13.5% — the behavioural effect that offsets savings and is often omitted from simpler cost estimates.

notes.quote: About 46 per cent ($16.9 billion) of total prescription drug expenditure was covered by public sources; 40 per cent ($14.7 billion) by private insurance; and the remaining 14 per cent ($4.9 billion) was paid for out-of-pocket.
notes.claim: PBO's baseline payer breakdown for 2021-22: of $36.6B in non-hospital prescription drug spending, 46% ($16.9B) public, 40% ($14.7B) private insurance, 14% ($4.9B) out-of-pocket — which is why expanding to single payer shifts cost rather than creating it, and why the private share is the source of the incremental public cost.

notes.quote: The economy-wide savings are projected to increase from $1.4 billion in 2024-25 to $2.2 billion in 2027-28, as the expenditure growth rate of Pharmacare is slower compared to the baseline (5.3 per cent vs. 5.8 per cent).
notes.claim: PBO: economy-wide savings under a single-payer plan are $1.4B in 2024-25 rising to $2.2B in 2027-28, because pharmacare's expenditure growth (5.3%) is slower than baseline (5.8%) as private plans grow faster than public ones.

notes.quote: Federal funding for National Pharmacare has been provided to Manitoba in support of no cost coverage of diabetes and birth control medications.
notes.claim: Manitoba's MEPP took effect 15 April 2025 (not June 2025 as the federal release anticipated) and covers birth control, diabetes, HIV prevention/treatment and HRT — but only diabetes and birth control are federally funded; Manitoba added HIV and HRT with its own money.

notes.quote: Present the prescription for an eligible MEPP product and your Manitoba Health card at a pharmacy.
notes.claim: Critical for the uptake question: there is no enrolment process. A patient presents a prescription and health card at a pharmacy and the pharmacist processes it — so the only possible usage measure is claims data, not an enrolment count, and no such series is published.

notes.quote: Ozempic was not included in the federal list of medications for no-cost coverage for discussion with provinces and territories.
notes.claim: Manitoba explicitly excludes Ozempic (semaglutide) from free coverage because it was not on the federal list — concrete evidence that the federal basket, not clinical need, determines what patients get.

notes.quote: MEPP covers the cost of eligible products (up to the lowest cost interchangeable product) and a professional fee of up to $14.
notes.claim: Manitoba covers only a $14 professional fee, capped at one fee per month for diabetes drugs and one per three months for oral contraceptives — a concrete illustration of the narrow, rationed shape of first-phase coverage.

notes.quote: Diabetes supplies remain as benefits under the Manitoba Pharmacare Program (where deductibles apply), and other provincial programs such as Employment and Income Assistance.
notes.claim: Diabetes supplies are NOT free under Manitoba's pharmacare; they remain benefits under the regular Manitoba Pharmacare Program where deductibles apply — so the federal device fund has not delivered free devices in Manitoba.

notes.quote: Beginning in Fiscal Year 2026-27, as a condition of annual funding under this Agreement, by October 1 of each Fiscal Year, Manitoba agrees to report to Canada the amount of Savings delivered to Manitoba Residents as a result of the measures taken to improve access to Diabetes Devices and Supplies under this Agreement (per section 2.1.b.), in respect of the preceding Fiscal Year.
notes.claim: The Manitoba agreement's reporting obligations require only attested financial statements and, for devices, the dollar "Savings" delivered. Nothing requires Manitoba to report how many people were covered or how many prescriptions were filled — which is why no enrolment or utilization series exists.

notes.quote: For the prescription drugs and related products included in Annex A, the amount of Fiscal Year 2022-23 spending by the Government of Manitoba was:
notes.claim: Annex B gives Manitoba's pre-agreement baseline: in 2022-23 the province already spent $23,945,982 on the Annex A drugs (diabetes $23,195,236, contraception $750,746) and $1,449,593 on insulin pumps and advanced glucose monitors. The federal Stream 1 allocation of ~$52.5-54.6M/yr is thus roughly double the province's existing spend.

notes.quote: The maximum amounts to be transferred to Manitoba over 4 years are:
notes.claim: The Manitoba agreement's exact Stream 1 allocations: $52,509,230 (2025-26), then $54,603,615 in each of 2026-27, 2027-28, 2028-29, plus a one-time $9,945,348 Stream 2 payment for diabetes devices in 2025-26 — about $225M total, consistent with the "more than $219 million" in the release.

notes.quote: Manitoba’s Implementation Date will be April 15, 2025.
notes.claim: Manitoba's Implementation Date is fixed in the agreement at 15 April 2025 — earlier than the federal news release's "June 2025" expectation, and evidence that provinces control timing.

notes.quote: levonorgestrel                                                         | Maximum of 3 treatments (3 tablets) per benefit year
notes.claim: The Manitoba Annex A diabetes list is broader than "first-line": it includes long-acting insulin degludec, SGLT-2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, canagliflozin), DPP-4 inhibitors and GLP-1 combination lixisenatide/glargine — though most newer agents require Exception Drug Status prior approval. Emergency contraception is capped at 3 treatments per benefit year.

notes.quote: Manitoba’s 2022-23 Stream 1 spending reported in _Annex B_ is greater than the amount reported under section 4.9.1.c.i.: Canada will withhold or reduce an amount equivalent to the difference between these two amounts, not exceeding the amount of funding received from Canada spent by Manitoba on product costs (4.9.1.b.i.) in the Fiscal Year;
notes.claim: The agreement contains an explicit anti-substitution mechanism: if Manitoba's Stream 1 spending from non-federal sources falls below its 2022-23 baseline, Canada withholds the difference. This addresses the concern that federal money might simply replace provincial spending.

report.body:
## TL;DR

The Pharmacare Act passed in October 2024, but what it delivered is a conditional funding framework for two therapeutic areas, not universal pharmacare: as of January 2026, four of thirteen provinces and territories — British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island and Yukon — had signed agreements worth just under a billion dollars over four years combined, covering a named list of contraceptives and diabetes products. No government publishes how many people use the program, and the funding agreements do not require them to: there is no enrolment step, only claims processed at pharmacy counters against a health card. On cost, the Parliamentary Budget Officer estimated a single-payer plan on the Quebec formulary at $11.2 billion incremental public cost in 2024-25 rising to $13.4 billion in 2027-28 — a combined federal-provincial figure the PBO explicitly declines to split — while its own expert committee put a narrower essential medicines list at $6–10 billion a year gross.

## Key Findings

- **The Act covers only contraception and diabetes in law.** Section 6(1) obliges the Minister to pay a province only where an agreement exists, and only for "specific prescription drugs and related products intended for contraception or the treatment of diabetes" [5]. It could be fully complied with while covering nothing else, indefinitely.
- **Four of thirteen jurisdictions have signed.** British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island and Yukon, per Health Canada as of 26 January 2026 [1]. Ontario, Quebec, Alberta, Saskatchewan, the Atlantic provinces and the two territories other than Yukon have no agreement.
- **The deals are small and back-loaded.** More than $670 million for BC over four years [2], more than $219 million for Manitoba [3], more than $30 million for PEI [4], up to $9.5 million for Yukon [7] — under a billion dollars combined, by my addition of the announcements.
- **Only PEI and Manitoba were paying claims through 2025.** Manitoba's Implementation Date is fixed at 15 April 2025 [16]; PEI's coverage began 1 May 2025 [4]; Yukon's no later than January 2026 [7]; BC's on 1 March 2026 [6].
- **Nobody counts users, by design.** Manitoba's process is to present a prescription and a health card at a pharmacy [15]; there is no enrolment. The agreements require financial statements and a dollar value of "Savings" on devices, not beneficiary counts [16].
- **The basket excludes some widely prescribed drugs.** Manitoba states Ozempic "was not included in the federal list of medications for no-cost coverage" [15], and that diabetes supplies remain subject to deductibles [15]. Emergency contraception is capped at three treatments per benefit year [16].
- **Provinces are expanding the basket at their own cost.** Manitoba funds HIV medications and hormone replacement therapy beyond the federally funded diabetes and birth control [15]; BC's agreement obliges free HRT from March 2026 [6].
- **Federal money is not simply replacing provincial money.** Manitoba spent $23,945,982 on the Annex A drugs in 2022-23 [16] against federal Stream 1 funding of $52,509,230 in 2025-26 [16], and the agreement contains an anti-substitution clause tied to that baseline [16].
- **The PBO puts a RAMQ-formulary plan at $11.2 billion incremental public cost in 2024-25, rising to $13.4 billion in 2027-28** [14] — federal and provincial combined, with the PBO stating it "is not possible to isolate federal costs" [14].
- **The same PBO model spans an order of magnitude depending on the basket:** $1.8 billion for a catastrophic formulary, $11.2 billion for RAMQ, and slightly *more* than baseline for an essential medicines list [14].
- **The government's own expert committee estimated $6–10 billion a year gross** for an essential medicines list [13], taking the PBO's 2023 work as its upper bound [13].
- **The committee found direct savings of up to $18 billion to public drug plans** [13] — a broader basket than its own cost estimate, so the two cannot be netted.

## Details

### 1. What the Pharmacare Act actually requires, and what it has delivered in law and institutions

The Pharmacare Act, S.C. 2024, c. 24, received royal assent on 10 October 2024. Its operative obligation is narrower than its name suggests. Section 6(1) does not create a national drug plan; it creates a conditional spending power:

> "**6** (1) The Minister must, if the Minister has entered into an agreement with a province or territory to do so, make payments to the province or territory in order to increase any existing public pharmacare coverage — and to provide universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage — for specific prescription drugs and related products intended for contraception or the treatment of diabetes." [5]

Three features of that drafting determine everything that follows. First, the federal duty to pay is triggered only by an agreement with a province or territory — no agreement, no obligation. Second, the coverage the money may buy is limited in the statute itself to contraception and diabetes products; the Act does not authorise federal funding for any other drug class. Third, the payment is conditional on the province delivering first-dollar coverage, meaning no deductible or co-payment at the point of use for the listed products.

The Act also imposes institutional duties. Section 11(1) required the Minister to establish a committee of experts within 30 days of royal assent:

> "**11** (1) The Minister must, no later than 30 days after the day on which this Act receives royal assent, establish a committee of experts, and provide for its membership, to make recommendations respecting options for the operation and financing of national, universal, single-payer pharmacare." [5]

Beyond that committee, the Act directs Canada's Drug Agency to develop a list of essential drugs and related products to inform a national formulary, a national bulk purchasing strategy, and a pan-Canadian strategy on appropriate prescribing, and it establishes a fund for diabetes devices and supplies [8].

The institutional gap is that the Act does not establish Canada's Drug Agency in law. Writing in the Canadian Medical Association Journal, health law and policy scholars made the point directly:

> "However, Bill C-64 does not establish the CDA by law, nor set out the agency’s powers, functions, and governance structures, which represents a missed opportunity to depoliticize the implementation and management of national pharmacare." [9]

That matters for the question of what has been delivered, because the agency that must produce the formulary the whole architecture depends on exists by federal announcement and budget appropriation, not by statute, and so is exposed to exactly the political direction the Act's proponents wanted to insulate it from. *Inference:* the Act is best read as a funding framework for a first phase plus a set of study and strategy obligations, not as the legal foundation of universal pharmacare. On its own terms it could be fully complied with while covering only contraception and diabetes, indefinitely.

### 2. Which provinces and territories have signed bilateral agreements, for how much, and on what conditions

As of Health Canada's page last updated 26 January 2026, four jurisdictions have signed national pharmacare bilateral agreements: British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island and Yukon. The page states plainly:

> "The Government of Canada has signed funding agreements with four provinces and territories to make a range of contraception and diabetes medications free." [1]

That is four of thirteen provinces and territories. The nine without an agreement include Ontario, Quebec, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Nunavut and the Northwest Territories — which between them hold the large majority of Canada's population. Alberta and Quebec in particular have publicly disputed the terms; Quebec's position is complicated by its existing provincial drug insurance regime, which the federal first-dollar condition would disrupt.

**Manitoba** signed first, on 27 February 2025. The federal contribution is more than $219 million over four years:

> "Through this first-ever national pharmacare agreement, the Government of Canada will provide more than $219 million over four years for universal coverage to a range of contraceptives and diabetes medications for Manitobans." [3]

The announcement anticipated coverage for the majority of products from June 2025 [3], but the agreement itself fixes the Implementation Date at 15 April 2025 [16] — earlier than announced. Manitoba also agreed to provide free hormone replacement therapy, an add-on beyond the federal contraception-and-diabetes template [15]. The agreement's own figures are $52,509,230 in Stream 1 funding for 2025-26 and $54,603,615 in each of the next three years, plus a one-time $9,945,348 for diabetes devices in 2025-26 [16].

**British Columbia** signed 6 March 2025, the largest of the four deals:

> "Today, the Honourable Mark Holland, Canada's Minister of Health, and the Honourable Josie Osborne, British Columbia's (BC) Minister of Health, announced the signing of a pharmacare agreement to invest more than $670 million over four years to provide universal access to contraceptive and diabetes medications, devices and supplies for residents of BC." [2]

The agreement text gives the exact federal allocations and shows how the money is back-loaded: $17,406,567 in fiscal 2025-26, then $204,948,289 in each of 2026-27, 2027-28 and 2028-29, plus a one-time $37,839,549 for diabetes devices in 2026-27 [6]. Adding those stated instalments gives roughly $670 million — my own arithmetic from the agreement's schedule, and it matches the "more than $670 million" in the news release [2]. The near-total absence of 2025-26 spending is not an error: BC's implementation date under the agreement is 1 March 2026, so the federal money only begins to flow in volume in the fiscal year the province actually starts paying for products.

BC's agreement also writes a provincial add-on into the federal terms:

> "Effective on March 1, 2026, British Columbia will provide free public coverage of hormone replacement therapies identified by British Columbia to treat menopausal symptoms for all Residents." [6]

**Prince Edward Island** signed in March 2025. The pharmacare component is more than $30 million over four years, part of a $40 million two-agreement package that also covers rare diseases:

> "Through the national pharmacare agreement, the Government of Canada will provide more than $30 million over four years for universal coverage to a range of contraceptives and diabetes medications for PEI residents, at little to no direct cost to them." [4]

PEI's coverage began 1 May 2025 — the earliest actual start date of the four.

**Yukon** signed 20 March 2025, the smallest deal:

> "announced the signing of a pharmacare agreement to invest up to $9.5 million over four years to provide universal access to contraceptive and diabetes medications for residents of Yukon." [7]

Yukon's coverage was to begin no later than January 2026 [7].

Two patterns are worth naming. The first is the timing gap between signature and delivery. Manitoba's binding Implementation Date is 15 April 2025 [16], PEI's coverage began 1 May 2025 [4], Yukon's no later than January 2026 [7], and BC's on 1 March 2026 [6]. For the first eighteen months after royal assent, the program was delivering coverage in two small provinces and one mid-sized one, while the largest deal sat dormant. The second is that the federal template is being amended at the provincial level: both Manitoba and BC extracted free hormone replacement therapy as a condition of signing [6][15], which is outside the Act's contraception-and-diabetes scope. *Inference:* that is a sign of provinces using their leverage in a voluntary, agreement-by-agreement structure, and it means "what pharmacare covers" already differs by province before universal pharmacare has been legislated at all.

### 3. What is covered: the contraception and diabetes drug and device list, and how coverage works in practice

What the program covers is defined as a named basket of products, not an open formulary or a therapeutic class. Health Canada's February 2024 backgrounder on contraception set out the list:

> "This includes oral contraceptives, copper and hormonal IUDs, injections, implants, rings, and morning-after pills." [10]

The accompanying diabetes announcement defined the other half of the basket as first-line glucose-lowering treatment:

> "Today’s announcement would ensure that, following agreement with PTs, diabetics in Canada will have access to first-line treatments for diabetes that lower blood glucose levels, including:" [11]

The items that follow that colon in the government's own document are insulin, metformin, sulfonylureas and SGLT-2 inhibitors, with specific brand and generic products named. Alongside the drugs sits a separate fund for diabetes devices and supplies — test strips, lancets, insulin pumps and advanced glucose monitors — which is why BC's agreement carries a distinct one-time $37,839,549 allocation for devices in 2026-27 [6].

**The actual coverage list is longer and more conditional than "first-line treatments" suggests.** The Manitoba agreement's Annex A is the operative legal list for that province, and it includes long-acting insulin degludec, the SGLT-2 inhibitors dapagliflozin, empagliflozin and canagliflozin, several DPP-4 inhibitors, and the GLP-1 combination lixisenatide with insulin glargine [16]. But most of the newer agents are listed as Exception Drug Status benefits, available only in exceptional circumstances with prior approval from Manitoba, while the open benefits are the older, cheaper products — the insulins, metformin, glyburide and gliclazide [16]. So the basket is not narrow in the sense of excluding modern drugs; it is narrow in the sense that modern drugs sit behind a prior-approval gate that older drugs do not.

**Some products are capped.** Emergency contraception is listed as an open benefit but with a hard limit: a "Maximum of 3 treatments (3 tablets) per benefit year" [16]. In practice Manitoba's program also caps the professional fee it will cover at $14, limited to once a month for diabetes medications and once every three months for oral contraceptives [15].

**Two exclusions matter more than the inclusions.** First, Ozempic (semaglutide) is not covered at no cost in Manitoba, and the province gives the reason plainly: "Ozempic was not included in the federal list of medications for no-cost coverage for discussion with provinces and territories." [15] The basket is federal, and it overrides clinical practice — semaglutide is widely prescribed for diabetes in Canada, and its absence is a direct consequence of the federal list, not a Manitoba judgement. Second, diabetes supplies are not free. Manitoba states that "Diabetes supplies remain as benefits under the Manitoba Pharmacare Program (where deductibles apply), and other provincial programs such as Employment and Income Assistance." [15] So the device half of the program, funded by a separate one-time federal payment, had not by 2026 delivered no-cost supplies in at least one of the four provinces; it expanded eligibility for pumps and monitors that were already covered subject to deductibles.

**Provinces are adding to the federal basket, not just implementing it.** Manitoba's program covers four categories — birth control, diabetes, HIV prevention and treatment, and hormone replacement therapy — but only two are federally funded: "Federal funding for National Pharmacare has been provided to Manitoba in support of no cost coverage of diabetes and birth control medications." [15] HIV medications and HRT are provincial additions. BC's agreement likewise obliges it to cover hormone replacement therapies from 1 March 2026 [6]. *Inference:* the voluntary, agreement-by-agreement structure gives provinces leverage to extract a broader provincial basket, so "what pharmacare covers" already varies by jurisdiction before any national formulary exists.

**On whether federal money substitutes for provincial spending**, the agreements are more careful than the public debate assumes. Manitoba's contains an explicit anti-substitution clause: if the province's own Stream 1 spending falls below its 2022-23 baseline, Canada withholds an equivalent amount [16]. The baseline is published in the agreement — Manitoba spent $23,945,982 on the Annex A drugs in 2022-23, of which just $750,746 was contraception [16]. Against that, the federal Stream 1 allocation is $52,509,230 in 2025-26 rising to $54,603,615 [16]. Federal money is therefore roughly double what the province previously spent on these products, which is consistent with genuine expansion rather than substitution — though the comparison is imperfect because the 2022-23 figure excludes what patients paid out of pocket.

### 4. How many people are actually using it: enrolment, claims and prescribing evidence

No federal or provincial government publishes a count of people using pharmacare. That is not a reporting failure that a better search would fix; it follows from how the program is built, and the design is documented.

**There is no enrolment.** Manitoba's program page describes the entire process: "Present the prescription for an eligible MEPP product and your Manitoba Health card at a pharmacy." [15] The pharmacist checks whether the person has 100 per cent coverage elsewhere, then processes the claim. Nobody signs up. Eligibility is having an active Manitoba Health card and not already being covered by a federal or another provincial plan [15]. Because there is no enrolment step, there is no register to count, and the only possible measure of use is claims data held by the province and its pharmacy network.

**The agreements do not require a headcount.** Manitoba's funding agreement obliges it, from fiscal 2026-27, to submit an attested financial statement showing how much federal money was received and spent on product costs [16], and to report the dollar value of "Savings" delivered on diabetes devices [16]. It does not require reporting of beneficiaries, prescription volumes or take-up rates. The federal government is therefore not collecting the number the question asks for, by design.

**What can be established is the ceiling on who could possibly use it.** As of the Health Canada page's last update on 26 January 2026, four jurisdictions had agreements [1], and residents of the other nine had no access at all. Within the four, coverage start dates are set in the agreements and staggered: Manitoba's Implementation Date is fixed at 15 April 2025 [16]; PEI's coverage began 1 May 2025 [4]; Yukon's no later than January 2026 [7]; BC's on 1 March 2026 [6]. Manitoba's start came earlier than the federal news release anticipated — the release said coverage was anticipated from June 2025 [3], while the binding agreement specifies 15 April 2025 [16] — which is a useful reminder that the agreement text, not the announcement, governs.

**The government's planning figures give intended scale, not measured use.** For BC: 1.3 million people for contraception and nearly 550,000 with diabetes [2]. For PEI: more than 41,000 for contraception and 16,000 with diabetes [4]. For Yukon: more than 12,000 and over 3,000 [7]. These are the eligible populations used to size the agreements. Summing the diabetes figures for BC, PEI and Yukon — Manitoba's release gives no comparable count [3] — gives a little over half a million people, against Health Canada's national figure that "About 3.8 million people in Canada have been diagnosed with diabetes" [12]. That is roughly an eighth of diagnosed Canadians, and only in the four jurisdictions, and only if every eligible person uses the program. That arithmetic is mine, not a government statement.

**A published baseline lets the fiscal question be answered even without a headcount.** Manitoba's Annex B discloses that the province spent $23,945,982 in 2022-23 on the drugs now in Annex A — $23,195,236 on diabetes and $750,746 on contraception — plus $1,449,593 on insulin pumps and advanced glucose monitors [16]. Those are the amounts a public plan paid, excluding patient copays and deductibles [16]. Since federal Stream 1 funding is $52,509,230 in 2025-26 [16], Ottawa is now paying roughly twice what Manitoba's public plan spent on the same products three years earlier, which is consistent with the program reaching people who were previously paying out of pocket rather than merely re-insuring the province. It also implies that the contraception basket was very cheap to a public plan before the program — under $1 million a year in Manitoba — which is the strongest available evidence that the pre-pharmacare barrier was patient cost, not public cost.

**Why first-year claims will understate need.** First-dollar coverage removes price only for people who already have a prescriber. Manitoba's own materials point to the gap: free birth control without a health card is available only through community health clinics and teen clinics [15], and a prescription is still required for emergency contraception — if the patient has none, a pharmacist may write one but may charge a fee that the program does not cover [15]. *Inference:* the population most likely to benefit — young people and people without a regular primary care provider — faces the highest non-price barriers, so early claims volumes will understate unmet need, and the absence of any published claims series makes the size of that gap unmeasurable from public sources.

### 5. What the Parliamentary Budget Officer and other independent estimates say full national pharmacare would cost

The Parliamentary Budget Officer's costing is the reference estimate, and it is more careful than the headline numbers usually quoted from it. The report is *Cost Estimate of a Single-payer Universal Drug Plan* (RP-2324-016-S), released 12 October 2023 — an update of the PBO's 2017 *Federal Cost of a National Pharmacare Program*. Its central finding:

> "Upon the implementation of a single-payer universal drug plan based on Quebec’s Régie de l’assurance maladie du Québec (RAMQ) formulary— “Pharmacare”—we estimate the incremental cost to the public sector (that is federal and provincial governments combined) to be $11.2 billion in 2024-25, increasing to $13.4 billion in 2027-28." [14]

**The PBO refuses to give a federal number, and says why.** This is the single most important caveat in the whole literature, and it is routinely ignored by people who attribute an "$11.2 billion federal cost" to the PBO:

> "As there is no certainty with respect to the federal and provincial shares of the cost of such a program, it is not possible to isolate federal costs." [14]

The $11.2 billion is a combined federal-plus-provincial figure. There is no PBO estimate of what Ottawa alone would pay, because that depends on a cost-sharing model no government has chosen.

**Gross and net differ by about $3.6 billion.** The PBO's own decomposition: total drug expenditure under pharmacare of $33.2 billion in 2024-25 rising to $38.9 billion in 2027-28; a gross cost incremental to existing public drug plans of $14.8 billion rising to $17.3 billion; and a net incremental public cost of $11.2 billion rising to $13.4 billion after crediting savings on direct federal spending and pharmacare copayment revenues [14]. So the gross incremental cost is "the cost of pharmacare" in one sense and the net is the cost in another, and the two differ by roughly a third.

**The PBO costed three different baskets, and the results differ by nearly an order of magnitude.** This is the answer to why published estimates disagree so wildly:

- **RAMQ formulary** (the full Quebec list, universal, with a $5 brand-name copay and exemptions): incremental public cost of $11.2 billion in 2024-25, $13.4 billion in 2027-28 [14].
- **Catastrophic formulary** (only drugs that could cause undue financial hardship, drawn from the catastrophic programs of BC, Ontario, Newfoundland and Labrador and PEI): incremental public cost of $1.8 billion in 2024-25 and $2.0 billion in 2027-28 [14].
- **Essential medicines formulary** (the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines adapted for Canada by researchers at St. Michael's Hospital in Toronto): drug expenditures of $0.4 billion and $0.3 billion *more* than the baseline in 2024-25 and 2027-28 [14].

That third result deserves emphasis because it cuts against the standard pharmacare argument. The PBO's explanation is that the list "consists primarily of generic drugs, the prices for which are already sufficiently low that little additional savings can be achieved with a single-payer plan." The higher expenditures are therefore the result of increased drug use that is not offset by negotiating savings [14].

**The National Pharmacare Committee of Experts adopted the PBO as its ceiling and produced a lower floor.** The committee, created under section 11 of the Act, reported in 2025 with a range:

> "The total cost of publicly funding a list of essential medicines will likely be between $6 to $10 billion dollars (see Appendix 2)." [13]

Its upper bound is explicitly the PBO's work: "We used the 2023 report from the Parliamentary Budget Office to estimate the upper bound of the cost of pharmacare." [13] Its lower bound is its own bottom-up model. It took the 185 essential medicines with multiple sources and no patent protection — the set the pan-Canadian Pharmaceutical Alliance identified as tendering candidates — and found that "In 2024, total spending on these 185 medicines was $12.6 billion." [13] It then applied generic pricing (−14%), lower public-plan markups (−17%) and competitive tendering (−40%) to reach $6.0 billion.

The tension between the committee's $6 billion floor and the PBO's finding that an essential medicines list costs slightly *more* than baseline is real and unresolved in the public documents. They are not the same calculation: the committee models a tendered, aggressively priced list and counts gross public cost; the PBO models the WHO-derived list against a status-quo baseline and counts the change. The committee's −40% tendering assumption is also contingent on a policy change not yet made — it notes that the pCPA's agreement to avoid competitive tendering expires in 2026 [13].

**On the savings side**, the committee estimates "direct savings of up to $18 billion to all public drug plans" [13], plus indirect savings from reduced hospitalisations "estimated to be larger than $1,000 per person per year for those currently unable to afford medicines" [13]. The $18 billion figure covers a far broader basket than the $6–10 billion cost estimate, so the two cannot be netted against each other; the $1,000 figure is a benefit estimate, not a fiscal offset, and is given without a source population or uncertainty range.

**Scale, for judging all of the above.** The committee reports that prescription drug spending from all payers rose from $34 billion in 2019 to $44 billion in 2024 [13], and puts the 2024 figure at about $45 billion, equal to roughly 11% of the federal budget:

> "The approximate $45 billion spent on prescription medicines (from all payers) in 2024 in Canada is similar to the amount spent on post-secondary education and more than the total budgets of Indigenous Services Canada, Health Canada, Veterans Affairs, the Department of Industry and the Mortgage and Housing Corporation combined." [13]

A $6–10 billion gross federal cost is therefore between roughly a seventh and a quarter of all-payer drug spending — large enough to be a genuine reallocation, and far short of absorbing the whole drug bill.

### 6. Reconciling the estimates: why the numbers differ, and what has actually been spent

The published estimates differ by more than an order of magnitude — from $1.8 billion to $17.3 billion for a first full year — and almost none of the spread comes from disagreement about drug prices. It comes from five choices, each of which is defensible on its own and rarely stated when a number is quoted.

**1. Which basket.** The PBO's three scenarios are the cleanest demonstration available. Same model, same data, same behavioural assumptions; changing only the formulary produces an incremental public cost of $1.8 billion (catastrophic), $11.2 billion (RAMQ) or roughly zero to negative (essential medicines) [14]. Any single figure for "the cost of pharmacare" is meaningless without naming the list, and most public discussion names none.

**2. Gross versus net.** The PBO's RAMQ scenario has a gross incremental cost of $14.8 billion and a net incremental public cost of $11.2 billion in the same year, the difference being savings on direct federal spending and copayment revenues [14]. Quoting either as "the cost" is defensible; quoting one and comparing it to an estimate built on the other is not.

**3. Whether the behavioural effect is counted.** The PBO assumes that cutting patient-borne prices by 47% to 100% raises prescription utilization by 13.5% [14]. That is a large, evidence-based, and easily omitted adjustment: an estimate that assumes utilization is fixed will understate the cost of any plan that removes copays. It is also the mechanism that explains why the essential medicines list costs *more* than baseline despite being made of cheap generics [14].

**4. What counts as a saving.** The PBO's economy-wide savings are modest and specific: $1.4 billion in 2024-25 rising to $2.2 billion in 2027-28, because pharmacare's expenditure growth of 5.3% is slower than the 5.8% baseline, as private plans historically grow faster than public ones [14]. Those are real resource savings to the economy. The committee's "$1,000 per person per year" [13] is a health-benefit estimate, not a resource saving, and the two get conflated constantly.

**5. The federal share, which nobody has costed.** Because the PBO declines to isolate federal costs [14], every claim about what Ottawa would spend on full pharmacare is an assumption about a cost-sharing formula, not an estimate.

**Why the public cost rises at all is worth stating plainly.** In 2021-22, of $36.6 billion in non-hospital prescription drug spending, 46% ($16.9 billion) was paid by public sources, 40% ($14.7 billion) by private insurance and 14% ($4.9 billion) out of pocket [14]. A single-payer plan does not create that spending; it transfers the private and out-of-pocket shares onto public books. That is why the incremental public cost is large while the economy-wide saving is small — the two numbers are measuring different things, and both are correct.

**What has actually been spent so far.** The commitments are small relative to any full-program estimate, and the payment schedules are back-loaded to match provincial start dates. Manitoba's Stream 1 allocation is $52,509,230 in 2025-26 rising to $54,603,615 in each of the following three years, plus a one-time $9,945,348 for diabetes devices [16]; its agreement began paying in June 2025, with half the first year's amount on signing and the balance in November [16]. BC receives $17,406,567 in 2025-26 against $204,948,289 in each of 2026-27 to 2028-29, plus $37,839,549 for devices [6] — because its implementation date is 1 March 2026 [6]. Adding the four published agreement values gives just under a billion dollars over four years: more than $670 million for BC [2], more than $219 million for Manitoba [3], more than $30 million for PEI [4] and up to $9.5 million for Yukon [7]. That total is my own addition of the announcements, not a government figure.

Two things follow. First, actual cash disbursed by early 2026 is necessarily a small fraction of that total, because three of the four provinces had barely started paying claims. Second, the scale is not comparable to the full-program estimates: under a billion dollars over four years for two therapeutic areas in four jurisdictions, against $6–10 billion a year gross for an essential medicines program covering 185 medicines, or $11.2–13.4 billion a year incremental public cost for a RAMQ-style plan [13][14]. The first phase is roughly two orders of magnitude below the full program in annual terms.

**For proportion, the committee's own comparison:**

> "The federal government has recently announced several new policies that advance national priorities related to equity including a dental care program and a childcare program (with annual costs estimated at $4.4 billion and $7.7 billion, respectively)." [13]

On the committee's range, full pharmacare sits between those two. It also identified plausible funding sources, noting that the exemption of employer contributions to private drug plans from income tax is worth about $5 billion a year and the exemption of prescription medicines from sales tax about $1.1 billion [13] — together covering the low end of its range.


## Beyond this question

The finding with the widest application is that the Pharmacare Act built a reporting regime that cannot answer the question its own preamble implies. The agreements require attested financial statements and, for devices, a dollar value of "Savings" delivered [16]. They require no beneficiary count, no prescription volume and no take-up measure. Anyone who wants to know whether pharmacare is working — a journalist, a legislator, a provincial auditor — is asking a question the funding architecture was not designed to answer. Adding a single reporting line to future agreements, requiring claims counts by product class, would cost almost nothing and settle in one year what this report cannot settle at all.

The second is that the federal basket is doing more work than the federal statute. Ozempic's exclusion from free coverage in Manitoba is attributed by the province directly to the federal list [15], not to clinical judgement. That means the essential medicines list the Canada's Drug Agency is developing [8] will determine, product by product, what Canadians can actually get — and it will do so without the agency having statutory powers or governance, as the CMAJ authors noted [9]. The most consequential document in Canadian drug policy over the next few years is a formulary being drafted by an agency that exists by appropriation rather than by law.
