Third, for anyone estimating costs: name the basket. The PBO's own scenarios span $1.8 billion to $11.2 billion for the same year with the same model [14]. A cost figure without a formulary attached is not an estimate of anything.

## Open questions

**How many people actually use the program.** No government publishes it, and the agreements do not require it [16]. Manitoba's Annex B baseline of $23,945,982 in 2022-23 spending on the Annex A drugs [16] permits an inference about public cost but not about patients. The first attested financial statements under the Manitoba agreement are due 1 October 2026 for fiscal 2025-26 [16]; even those will report dollars, not people.

**Whether the four agreements are the end of the first phase or all of it.** Nine jurisdictions, including Ontario, Quebec and Alberta, have no agreement. No public document states whether negotiations are active, stalled or abandoned. A reader should treat "four of thirteen" as the state of the record on 26 January 2026 [1], not as a settled endpoint.

**Whether federal money substitutes for provincial spending.** The Manitoba agreement contains an anti-substitution clause tied to a published 2022-23 baseline [16], which is real protection. Whether the BC, PEI and Yukon agreements carry equivalent clauses with equivalent baselines is not something I verified; each agreement would need reading in full.

**The committee's $6 billion floor versus the PBO's essential-medicines result.** The committee models tendered prices and finds $6–10 billion [13]; the PBO models the WHO-derived list against baseline and finds it costs slightly more than status quo [14]. Both cannot describe the same policy. Resolving this requires the committee's Appendix 2 methodology and the PBO's assumptions read side by side, which I did not do in full.

**Whether the Committee of Experts' report has been responded to.** The Act required the committee to report within a year [5]; it reported in 2025. Whether the government has formally responded, accepted or set aside its recommendations is not established here.

**Coverage note.** The evidence base for this report is thin in one specific respect worth stating: of the sources cited, the large majority are Government of Canada publications — the Act, Health Canada releases, the bilateral agreement texts and the committee report — with the PBO and one CMAJ analysis providing the independent or arms-length checks. The PBO is an officer of Parliament and independent of the government it costs; the CMAJ piece is peer-reviewed. But on questions of what provinces are actually delivering, the only detailed primary source I read in full was Manitoba's. BC, PEI and Yukon program pages were not read, so the Manitoba findings on exclusions, caps and supply coverage should not be generalized to the other three provinces without checking.

It explicitly extends beyond phones to other smart technology, and it closes the bring-your-own-device loophole by providing that BYOD schemes must not include mobile phones [10].

The guidance became statutory on 29 June 2026, to be followed from 1 September 2026 [10] — which matters for the evidence, because it means the English studies reviewed below were conducted under a pre-statutory regime of voluntary school policies, not under the current national rule. **Victoria** is the strongest legal form among the jurisdictions examined here.

Restriction is a requirement of the Education and Training Reform Act 2006 and Ministerial Order No. 1515, applying to all government, Catholic and independent schools, not government schools alone [18].

From the start of 2027, phones and smart glasses brought to school must be switched off and stored in a way that restricts student access; wearables must have notifications, cellular connection and recording functions off during school hours; and personal audio devices must not be used during school hours [18].
The stated aims are to reduce health, safety and privacy risks, reduce classroom distraction, and promote social interaction and physical activity at break [18].

The policy was announced in November 2022 and mandated from Term 1 2023 in public secondary schools, requiring students to keep their personal devices "off and away between the start and end of each school day and while attending authorized school activities off-site" [12].
It is bell-to-bell and it is enforced with hardware: schools used the Yondr magnetically locked pouch [12].

The mobile-free school policy was introduced in January 2024; a representative baseline measurement followed in the summer of 2024; and the Ministry signalled that by summer 2025 it would work with primary, secondary and special education stakeholders to "assess if additional measures, such as a legal ban, are needed" [16].

The reported early findings were qualitative and favourable — schools valued having one national guideline to anchor conversations with students, parents and teachers, high school students were "interacting more socially with each other, and lessons are more focused" [16] — but these are impressions from a baseline, not outcome estimates, and the Dutch study discussed below found no wellbeing or bullying differences while finding that full bans were associated with lower student–teacher connectedness [14]. **The United States** has moved by volume rather than by national rule, since education is not federal.
As of August 2026, 39 states and the District of Columbia require districts to restrict student cellphone use [17].

The state mandates cluster at the stricter end: "bell-to-bell" bans, running from the first bell to dismissal with no lunch or break exception, are the most common form of state law mandate, though the storage decision is usually left local — student keeps the device, classroom collection, or individual locked storage [17].

King and colleagues' own summary of the field is that the emerging picture is of "no detectable effects or relatively subtle effects detected only in certain subgroups over longer periods of time" [12].

Across 1,227 pupils aged 12 to 15 in 30 English secondary schools, mean score on the Warwick–Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale was 47 (SD 9), with no evidence of a difference between restrictive and permissive schools: adjusted mean difference −0.48, 95% CI −2.05 to 1.06, p = 0.62 [9].

The same study did find that higher social media posting frequency was associated with greater psychological distress and with self-harm thoughts and behaviours, and its authors drew the same conclusion as the English team — the association is with the behaviour, and the school ban does not reach it [5].

Reviewing what existed, the authors record that "Two studies found no significant effects of smartphone bans at school on students’ well-being (Guldvik & Kvinnsland, 2018; Goodyear et al., 2025), while another reported reduced mental health care needs for girls only (Abrahamsson, 2024)." [2].
Abrahamsson's abstract reports three movements in the same direction — lower psychological health care use among girls, lower bullying for both genders, and better grade point averages for girls [6].

Comparing full school-grounds bans with classroom-only bans, it found no significant differences in wellbeing or bullying, but full bans were associated with lower student–teacher connectedness and, for girls, reduced school belonging [14].

Ferguson makes this argument directly and it is the sharpest statement of the problem: "Unfortunately, the wide proliferation of smartphone bans without evidence may make true randomized-controlled trials unlikely at this juncture, given that it may be increasingly difficult to locate schools systematically that have not been touched by such bans" [8].
Indeed, several recent reviews of research in this area have shown that evidence supporting the efficacy of such bans is limited" [8].

The most recent United States causal study uses synthetic difference-in-differences on the National Survey of Children's Health from 2016 to 2024, and states its own fragility: "Currently, there are data for only one state with two post-ban periods and two states with one post-ban period, which makes the results preliminary evidence only" [4].

Using administrative and survey data: "Using administrative and survey data with an event-study design, I show that banning smartphones in middle schools has no average effect on education or mental health but masks important gender differences" [6].

As the US inventory shows, state mandates cluster on bell-to-bell rules but usually leave the storage decision local — student keeps the device, classroom collection, or individual locked storage [17].
South Australia avoided this by specifying the hardware [12]; England's statutory guidance specifies the default but leaves enforcement to schools [10].
Teen support falls sharply as restrictions tighten: "just 17 percent of teens supported bell-to-bell bans, compared with 41 percent of teens who supported instructional-time bans" [17].

The South Australian compliance figure of 87% under locked pouches [12] suggests that enforcement technology can substitute for consent, at least in the short run, but nobody has measured whether that holds over years.

notes.quote: Furthermore, in-school and out of school phone use are positively correlated, which suggests that in-school and out of school phone/media use behaviours are comparable.
notes.claim: The authors' explanation for the null is not displacement: in-school use is only a small share of total use, and in-school and out-of-school use are positively correlated (heavy in-school users are heavy out-of-school users), so removing in-school use cannot move the total much.

Within the same study, in-school smartphone time was itself significantly associated with greater classroom disruptiveness (adjusted 0.22 PBQ points per hour, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.31, p<0.0001; standardized 0.14), i.e. device use in school does track disruptiveness — a finding the section leaves out while arguing the device in the room is irrelevant.

notes.quote: Beland and Murphy estimated the impact of banning phones for low-achieving students was the equivalent of an additional hour a week in school
notes.claim: The Beland & Murphy effect size in time terms: equivalent to an additional hour a week in school or five extra school days a year for low-achieving students.

report.body:
## TL;DR

School smartphone bans are now near-universal policy in the rich democracies — England made them statutory guidance in 2026, Victoria enforces them by ministerial order, the Netherlands and Ontario use non-statutory direction, South Australia mandated them from Term 1 2023, and 39 US states plus DC require districts to restrict phones — but the instruments differ so much in span and enforcement that "ban" is not one treatment. The best evidence finds that restrictive school policies do not measurably change mental wellbeing, classroom disruptiveness, bullying or academic engagement, while the same studies repeatedly find that individual phone and social media use is associated with worse outcomes on every one of those measures. The one well-known positive result — Beland and Murphy's English attainment gain, concentrated among low achievers at about a week of extra schooling a year — failed to replicate in a Swedish study with more than ten times the schools. Nobody has measured attention directly, and no study has yet tested exam results against the post-2022 wave of bans.

## Key Findings

- **Bans do not measurably change mental wellbeing.** SMART Schools (England, 30 schools, 1,227 pupils aged 12–15) found no difference between restrictive and permissive policies: adjusted mean difference on the Warwick–Edinburgh scale −0.48, 95% CI −2.05 to 1.06, p = 0.62 [9]. Iceland's difference-in-differences study (70 schools, 23,938 observations) found no meaningful change in depressive symptoms, anxiety, hostility or wellbeing [11].
- **Bans do not measurably change classroom behaviour.** SMART Schools' effect on disruptiveness was 0.06 points, 95% CI −0.57 to 0.68, standardized 0.03 (−0.25 to 0.30), on 1,096 pupils [7].
- **The exposure gradient and the policy effect disagree.** Within the same studies, more phone and social media time is associated with more disruption [7] and more distress [5], yet the policy that is meant to reduce exposure shows no effect on the outcome — and restrictive schools show lower in-school use but no difference in overall weekday or weekend use [9].
- **Bullying evidence is contradictory and splits by measurement.** Iceland found no difference in cyberbullying or in-person bullying [11]; a Spanish quasi-experiment using official Ministry of Education bullying reports found a 15–18% reduction in incidence among 12–17-year-olds [12]. The Spanish result measures recorded incidents, the Icelandic one measures pupils' own reports.
- **The attainment claim rests on one study that did not replicate.** Beland and Murphy found gains concentrated among lower-achieving English pupils, worth about an extra hour a week in school [12][13]; Kessel, Hardardottir and Tyrefors, using 1,086 Swedish schools, found no improvement, robust to ban timing, urban setting and socioeconomic status [15].
- **Effects, where found, are in subgroups rather than averages.** Abrahamsson's Norwegian event study found no average effect on education or mental health but "masks important gender differences" — reduced psychological health care use and better GPAs for girls, lower bullying for both genders [6].
- **The strongest legal instruments are the least evaluated.** Victoria's restriction is a requirement of the Education and Training Reform Act 2006 and Ministerial Order 1515 [18]; South Australia's bell-to-bell rule with Yondr locked pouches is the strictest configuration independently evaluated [12]. England's statutory guidance took effect in 2026, after the studies reviewed here were conducted [10].
- **Attention is the construct least measured.** No study in this set uses a behavioural or cognitive attention task; "attention" is operationalised as teacher- or pupil-reported disruptiveness [7].
- **A true trial is now probably impossible.** Ferguson: the proliferation of bans "may make true randomized-controlled trials unlikely at this juncture" [8].

## Details

### 1. Which jurisdictions have adopted school smartphone bans, and what does each instrument actually require

The first thing to establish is that "ban" covers instruments with very different reach, and most of the disagreement in this literature dissolves once you separate them. Three dimensions vary independently: the legal form (statute, ministerial order, statutory guidance, or non-statutory expectation), the span of the school day covered (classroom time only, or bell-to-bell including breaks), and whether the device is merely unusable or physically confiscated. A study of one configuration does not license conclusions about another.

**Ontario** sits at the permissive end on span and the weak end on legal form. The instrument is Policy/Program Memorandum 128, issued 27 June 2024 and effective 1 September 2024, replacing an earlier 2019 version. It is a provincial Code of Conduct made under section 301(1) of the Education Act — direction to school boards, not a statute [3]. Its rule is age-tiered: "Students Grade 7 and above may not use cellphones or other mobiles devices during class time without the explicit permission of their teacher. Students Grade 6 and below may not use cellphones or other mobile devices at school during the school day without the permission of a teacher" [1]. The operative words are "may not use": students keep their devices. The memorandum requires boards to have local policies that at minimum require that for grades 7 to 12 students' devices "are stored out of view and powered off or set to silent mode during instructional time, except when their use is explicitly permitted by the educator" [3]. Breaks, lunch and the corridor are outside the provincial restriction for secondary pupils, and enforcement is delegated to boards and, in practice, to individual teachers.

**England** is the opposite on span and uses a distinctive legal form. The Department for Education's guidance covers the full day: "This publication provides statutory guidance to individual schools and trusts on how to implement a policy that prohibits the use of mobile phones throughout the school day, including during lessons, the time between lessons, breaktimes and lunchtime" [10]. The default is stated absolutely: "All schools should be mobile phone-free environments by default; anything other than this should be by exception only" [10]. Two features are unusual and worth noting. It explicitly extends beyond phones to other smart technology, and it closes the bring-your-own-device loophole by providing that BYOD schemes must not include mobile phones [10]. The guidance became statutory on 29 June 2026, to be followed from 1 September 2026 [10] — which matters for the evidence, because it means the English studies reviewed below were conducted under a pre-statutory regime of voluntary school policies, not under the current national rule.

**Victoria** is the strongest legal form among the jurisdictions examined here. Restriction is a requirement of the Education and Training Reform Act 2006 and Ministerial Order No. 1515, applying to all government, Catholic and independent schools, not government schools alone [18]. Its scope has also been widened beyond phones to smart glasses, smart watches and personal audio devices. From the start of 2027, phones and smart glasses brought to school must be switched off and stored in a way that restricts student access; wearables must have notifications, cellular connection and recording functions off during school hours; and personal audio devices must not be used during school hours [18]. The stated aims are to reduce health, safety and privacy risks, reduce classroom distraction, and promote social interaction and physical activity at break [18]. Victoria is also the clearest case of a policy justified on grounds wider than learning — privacy and safety are named first.

**South Australia** was among the earliest of the current wave and has the most evaluated implementation. The policy was announced in November 2022 and mandated from Term 1 2023 in public secondary schools, requiring students to keep their personal devices "off and away between the start and end of each school day and while attending authorized school activities off-site" [12]. It is bell-to-bell and it is enforced with hardware: schools used the Yondr magnetically locked pouch [12]. That combination — full-day span plus physical inaccessibility — makes South Australia the strictest configuration that has been independently evaluated, which is why the null results discussed below carry particular weight.

**The Netherlands** took the non-statutory route first and is now considering escalation. The mobile-free school policy was introduced in January 2024; a representative baseline measurement followed in the summer of 2024; and the Ministry signalled that by summer 2025 it would work with primary, secondary and special education stakeholders to "assess if additional measures, such as a legal ban, are needed" [16]. The reported early findings were qualitative and favourable — schools valued having one national guideline to anchor conversations with students, parents and teachers, high school students were "interacting more socially with each other, and lessons are more focused" [16] — but these are impressions from a baseline, not outcome estimates, and the Dutch study discussed below found no wellbeing or bullying differences while finding that full bans were associated with lower student–teacher connectedness [14].

**The United States** has moved by volume rather than by national rule, since education is not federal. As of August 2026, 39 states and the District of Columbia require districts to restrict student cellphone use [17]. The state mandates cluster at the stricter end: "bell-to-bell" bans, running from the first bell to dismissal with no lunch or break exception, are the most common form of state law mandate, though the storage decision is usually left local — student keeps the device, classroom collection, or individual locked storage [17]. Two schools under the same state law can therefore deliver different experiences, which is a serious problem for any evaluation that treats "ban state" as a treatment.

**Globally**, the count is uncertain and the most-cited figure is second-hand. A 2026 study of Dutch schools reports that "Around 40% of countries in the world (e.g., the Netherlands, Belgium, France, Israel, Turkey, Bangladesh, the United States, and certain areas in Canada and Australia) have enacted laws restricting smartphone use during school hours (UNESCO, 2023)" [14]. This is UNESCO's 2023 Global Education Monitoring Report cited at second hand, and it should be treated as an order-of-magnitude figure rather than a precise count, because the category of laws restricting smartphone use during school hours bundles together instruments as different as Victoria's ministerial order and a national recommendation. Within Canada, the picture is provincial and fragmented: Ontario's memorandum is one instrument among several, and the UNESCO list refers only to "certain areas."

The variation has a consequence that runs through everything below. The restrictive condition in the English evidence is a school's own voluntary policy; in South Australia it is a mandated bell-to-bell rule with locked pouches; in Ontario it is a class-time use restriction with the device in the pupil's pocket. These are not the same treatment, and a null in one does not establish a null in another. There is also a legitimacy dimension: Child Trends reports that in 2026 Pew found "just 17 percent of teens supported bell-to-bell bans, compared with 41 percent of teens who supported instructional-time bans" [17]. The configurations that are strictest on paper are the least supported by the people subject to them, which is exactly the condition under which compliance decays.

### 2. What have evaluations measured about learning and academic performance

The learning literature is dominated by one study and defined by the difficulty of replicating it.

Beland and Murphy's study of English schools is the origin of the claim that phone bans raise attainment. It analysed 90 schools in the United Kingdom that had implemented bans between 2006 and 2010, using school policy surveys matched to administrative exam records, and its core finding is that "student performance in high stakes exams significantly increases post ban" [13]. The effect was not uniform. As summarised by King and colleagues, "The authors reported an improvement in student academic performance among lower-achieving students following the ban, whereas the high achievers were neither positively nor negatively affected" [12]. The magnitude is usually expressed in time rather than standard deviations: the gain for low-achieving pupils was equivalent to an additional hour a week in school, or five additional school days a year [12]. That is a modest effect, and it is worth holding onto the number, because the popular version of this finding is considerably larger than the finding.

The replication failed. Kessel, Hardardottir and Tyrefors applied the same logic to Sweden with a far larger sample: "Kessel, Hardardottir, and Tyrefors (2020) attempted to replicate Beland and Murphy's study in their study of 1,086 schools in Sweden. In contrast to Beland and Murphy's study, Kessel et al. reported no improvement in student performance in schools with a phone ban. Taking into consideration the timing of the ban, urban versus non-urban school setting, and socioeconomic status did not affect the pattern of results" [15]. More than ten times the schools (1,086 against 90 — my own calculation from the two sample sizes), a null, and a null that held across the pre-specified moderators. This is the single most important pair of results in the field, and it is not a story of one study refuting another. It is a story about how much the effect depends on context.

The most plausible reading is that the English result is real but conditional, and the conditions were specific. England in 2006–2010 had a particular exam structure, a particular pattern of when schools adopted policies, and a particular baseline of phone use — pre-smartphone saturation for part of the period. Beland and Murphy's design exploited variation in *when* schools adopted bans, which is vulnerable to the possibility that schools adopt bans at moments of wider change: a new head teacher, a behaviour crackdown, an inspection. If the schools that banned phones were also the schools reforming behaviour policy, the estimated effect is the reform, not the phone. The Swedish null, in a system where bans were also adopted endogenously, suggests exactly that.

The Australian and English nulls on engagement point the same way. In the South Australian preregistered natural experiment, "Linear mixed models indicated that ban and no ban school groups did not differ significantly in terms of problematic phone use, academic engagement, and school belonging" [12]. Academic engagement is not attainment, and no study in this set reports exam results from the current wave of post-2022 bans, which means the attainment question has not been tested on the smartphone-saturated school population that the current policies actually govern. Beland and Murphy's data are from an era when a phone in a classroom was a phone, not a portal; that is a genuine limit on transferring their result to 2026.

The recent review-level summaries converge on the same position. King and colleagues, reviewing the field, conclude that "Although studies are not entirely consistent, the emerging research picture is that mobile phone bans appear to have either no detectable effects or relatively subtle effects detected only in certain subgroups over longer periods of time" [12]. Ferguson states it more bluntly: "In truth, such policies have been put into place despite little evidence that such bans promote student wellbeing or grades. Indeed, several recent reviews of research in this area have shown that evidence supporting the efficacy of such bans is limited" [8].

One further result complicates the "no effect" reading and should be kept alongside it. In the Norwegian event study, the average effect on education was null but the gender-specific effects were not — Abrahamsson reports better grade point averages for girls [6]. Taken with Beland and Murphy's concentration of gains among low achievers, the pattern across the two most credible positive studies is that effects, where they appear, are in subgroups rather than averages. That is a substantively different claim from "bans raise attainment," and it implies that a jurisdiction evaluating its own ban should pre-specify which pupils it expects to benefit rather than looking for a mean shift.

The honest summary for a policymaker is that the strongest evidence for an attainment effect comes from one country in one period, at a magnitude of roughly a week of extra schooling per year for the pupils already struggling most; the closest replication, in a different country with more schools, found nothing; and nothing in the post-smartphone wave of bans has yet been tested against exam results at all.

### 3. What have evaluations measured about attention, distraction and classroom behaviour

The most direct measurement of attention and classroom behaviour comes from SMART Schools, the England study, and its result is a precisely estimated null. SMART Schools compared 30 secondary schools — 20 with restrictive phone policies and 10 permissive — surveying 1,227 pupils aged 12 to 15 in 2022–23. On the Pupil Behaviour Questionnaire measure of classroom disruptiveness, the adjusted mean difference between restrictive and permissive schools was 0.06 points, 95% CI −0.57 to 0.68, p = 0.88; standardized, 0.03, 95% CI −0.25 to 0.30, on 1,096 pupils [7]. The confidence interval is narrow enough to exclude anything but a small effect. Whatever restrictive policies are doing, they are not measurably reducing how disruptive lessons are.

That null sits alongside a strong association at the level of the individual pupil, and the contrast is the most analytically interesting finding in the literature. Within the same study, increases in smartphone and social media time were associated with increases in disruptive classroom behaviour across every period measured — in school, on weekdays, at weekends, and week-on-week [7]. So the exposure-outcome gradient is real and consistent, while the policy lever that is supposed to move the exposure produces no detectable change in the outcome. The authors put the two side by side explicitly: they observed no significant differences in "anxiety, depression, problematic social media use, sleep, physical activity, attainment, and disruptive behaviour when comparing adolescents exposed to restrictive or permissive school phone policies, but we did observe significant negative associations between these out- comes and increasing phone and social media time" [7].

The mechanism that reconciles the two is displacement rather than reduction. Restrictive schools in SMART Schools did report lower in-school phone and social media use, but there was no difference between restrictive and permissive schools in overall weekday or weekend use [9]. A ban moves the phone use to the margins of the school day and to the evening; it does not reduce the total dose. If disruptive classroom behaviour is driven by total use, sleep loss, or the state a pupil arrives in rather than by the device in the room, a class-time restriction would be expected to show exactly the pattern observed: lower in-school use, unchanged behaviour.

This is an inference from the pattern rather than a measured mechanism, and it is worth flagging as such. SMART Schools was cross-sectional, so it cannot distinguish a school that adopted a restrictive policy because its behaviour was already poor from one whose behaviour was unaffected by the policy. A school with a disorderly corridor problem is plausibly more likely to ban phones, which would bias the comparison toward showing bans doing nothing or worse. The authors do not report an analysis that rules this out, and the small number of schools (30) means school-level confounding cannot be adjusted away.

Nothing in this literature measures attention directly — no sustained-attention task, no classroom observation of on-task time, no measure of mind-wandering. "Attention" in these studies is operationalised as teacher- or pupil-reported disruptiveness. That is a substantial gap between the policy debate, which is conducted almost entirely in the vocabulary of attention and focus, and the measurement, which is about conduct.

Two further measurements belong here. The first is a scale check on how much in-school exposure a ban is actually addressing. The Icelandic authors report that "Recent data show that adolescents spend more than 1 hour per day on smartphones during school hours, with social media accounting for the largest use" [11]. An hour a day is a real dose, and it is the dose a bell-to-bell ban is designed to eliminate. That the eliminations produced no measurable behavioural change in the English and Icelandic studies is therefore not a story about a trivial exposure.

The second is compliance, which is the mechanism on which every one of these nulls depends. South Australia is the only jurisdiction in this set where compliance was measured alongside outcomes, and the result was high: schools used the Yondr magnetically locked pouch, and "The present study found that most students (87%) reportedly complied with the ban" [12]. Non-compliance was patterned rather than random — predicted by older age, higher social media posting frequency, prior in-school phone use, and having experienced bullying [12]. That last predictor is substantively important: the pupils most likely to keep a phone at school are, in part, those for whom school feels unsafe. A ban enforced without attention to that group may remove the device from exactly the pupils using it as a safety line.

Finally, this question should be set against what the record already establishes about the mechanism most often invoked to explain why a phone in a classroom damages attention. The "brain drain" account — that the mere presence of a device consumes working memory — has not held up in the record's own screens evidence review, which found that a pre-registered direct replication failed and that the largest meta-analysis found no effect of mere presence. Given that, the plausible channel from phone to attention is not passive presence but active use and its displacement of sleep, and a ban that leaves total use unchanged would be expected to do little. This is why the SMART Schools pattern — lower in-school use, unchanged overall use, unchanged behaviour — is coherent rather than surprising.

### 4. What have evaluations measured about bullying and cyberbullying

Bullying is where the evidence is most contested, and the two strongest studies point in opposite directions. The disagreement appears to track measurement method more than geography, which is the thing to watch.

The largest study is Icelandic and it is a difference-in-differences design: 70 schools, 23,938 adolescent observations, with 22 schools adopting bans between 2018 and 2023 and the rest acting as comparison. It found nothing. The authors' conclusion is unambiguous: "We also found no evidence of meaningful differences in the experience of cyberbullying or in-person bullying in schools with and without phone bans" [11]. They offer a mechanism for the null that is worth taking seriously — that online and offline bullying involve largely the same individuals, so removing the device from the school day does not remove the conflict, it relocates it. A pupil who is being bullied in the corridor is being bullied by the same people on the platform that evening.

The main positive finding comes from Spain. Regional bans were evaluated using official bullying reports collected by the Spanish Ministry of Education, and the result was a 15 to 18 per cent reduction in bullying incidence among students aged 12 to 17, and a 10 to 18 per cent reduction among 15- to 17-year-olds [12]. This is a quasi-experiment using administrative data rather than a randomised design, and it is reported here via King and colleagues' summary rather than from the original paper — a limitation of this section that should be checked against Beneito and Vicente-Chirivella's own tables before the figure is relied on.

The obvious reconciliation is that the two studies measure different things. Iceland surveyed adolescents about their own experience of being bullied, which captures the subjective and relational event wherever it happens. Spain counted official bullying reports, which capture what a school records and acts on. A ban plausibly reduces the visibility of bullying inside school — phones out of sight mean fewer incidents witnessed and reported on school premises — without reducing the underlying rate of victimisation. Under that reading, the Spanish result is a measurement of institutional recording as much as of pupil experience, and the Icelandic result is the more credible estimate of what pupils actually endure. That is my inference, not a finding either paper states, and it is the single most important thing to test in this literature.

No study in this set reports a bullying outcome by type with adequate power to separate cyber from in-person, despite the theoretical case that a school ban should act far more strongly on the former. The Icelandic authors' finding of no difference in either category is therefore the strongest available evidence, and it cuts against the mechanism the policy assumes.

The South Australian study adds a third measurement and a detail that complicates the Spanish reading. Bullying was slightly higher in the ban group at baseline, but bullying decreased significantly in both groups over the study period [12]. A fall in both arms is not evidence for the ban, and a baseline difference that favours the comparison group is exactly the confounding that non-random assignment produces. King and colleagues' own summary of the field is that the emerging picture is of "no detectable effects or relatively subtle effects detected only in certain subgroups over longer periods of time" [12].

The measurement question is therefore the crux, and it has a clear test. The Spanish data count incidents the school records; the Icelandic data ask pupils whether they were bullied. A school that removes phones from the premises plausibly records fewer phone-mediated incidents — a real change in the school's administrative reality, and possibly a real change in the school's climate — without any change in what a pupil experiences in the evening. Both results can be true, and the policy question is which one the ban is supposed to deliver. If the aim is to reduce recorded incidents on school grounds, Spain suggests it can. If the aim is to reduce adolescent suffering, Iceland suggests it does not.

### 5. What have evaluations measured about mental health and wellbeing

Mental health is the outcome the policy is most often justified by, and it is the outcome where the nulls are most consistent. Four separate studies, in three countries, using different designs, fail to find that school bans improve wellbeing.

The best-powered is SMART Schools. Across 1,227 pupils aged 12 to 15 in 30 English secondary schools, mean score on the Warwick–Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale was 47 (SD 9), with no evidence of a difference between restrictive and permissive schools: adjusted mean difference −0.48, 95% CI −2.05 to 1.06, p = 0.62 [9]. The authors state the conclusion plainly: "There is no evidence that restrictive school policies are associated with overall phone and social media use or better mental wellbeing in adolescents. The findings do not provide evidence to support the use of school policies that prohibit phone use during the school day in their current form, and indicate that these policies require further development" [9]. Two things in that sentence matter. The null is on both wellbeing and total use — the policy did not shift the overall dose, only its timing and location. And the authors' own reading is not that bans are harmful but that the form of prohibition tested is not doing the work.

The South Australian study is a prospective design with before-and-after measurement: 5 schools, 1,319 students at baseline and 603 at follow-up. It too found nothing on mental health: "No significant differences in mental health outcomes were found between ban versus no-ban groups based on social media posting levels" [5]. The same study did find that higher social media posting frequency was associated with greater psychological distress and with self-harm thoughts and behaviours, and its authors drew the same conclusion as the English team — the association is with the behaviour, and the school ban does not reach it [5].

The Dutch literature summary adds a fourth data point and a note of genuine heterogeneity. Reviewing what existed, the authors record that "Two studies found no significant effects of smartphone bans at school on students’ well-being (Guldvik & Kvinnsland, 2018; Goodyear et al., 2025), while another reported reduced mental health care needs for girls only (Abrahamsson, 2024)." [2]. The Swedish and Norwegian finding of a girls-only effect is the one result in this literature that survives as a positive mental health finding, and it is important to be precise about what it is: a reduction in contact with health care services, not a measured improvement in wellbeing. Service use is a joint product of need, access, referral thresholds and help-seeking, and a girls-only reduction is compatible with several mechanisms that have nothing to do with phones.

The consistent pattern across these studies is a dissociation between the exposure gradient and the policy effect. Every study that measures individual phone or social media use finds it associated with worse mental health; no study that compares school policies finds the policy moving the outcome. That is the same structure seen in the behaviour results, and it points to the same inference: the association is with total use, which school-hour restrictions do not materially reduce. The inference is mine; the studies report the two findings without asserting the causal link between them.

Two cautions apply to all four. Every one is observational, and the two largest are cross-sectional comparisons of schools that chose their own policies. Schools that adopt restrictive policies may differ systematically from those that do not — in intake, in discipline culture, in how much staff time they can spend enforcing rules — and none of these studies can fully remove that. And mental wellbeing measured on a population scale moves slowly; a policy introduced in one academic year, measured in the same year, has limited opportunity to show an effect on a construct that is partly trait-like. A null at twelve months is not a null at five years.

The Norwegian detail is worth spelling out because it shows what a heterogeneous result looks like in practice. Abrahamsson's abstract reports three movements in the same direction — lower psychological health care use among girls, lower bullying for both genders, and better grade point averages for girls [6]. Lower bullying for both genders is the one result here that directly contradicts the Icelandic null, and it is the strongest single piece of evidence that a ban can move a social outcome — though it sits in a study whose average effect was zero, which means the bullying reduction was concentrated rather than general.

The Dutch study supplies the one finding in this literature that runs against the policy. Comparing full school-grounds bans with classroom-only bans, it found no significant differences in wellbeing or bullying, but full bans were associated with lower student–teacher connectedness and, for girls, reduced school belonging [14]. Connectedness and belonging are not peripheral: they are among the strongest known correlates of adolescent mental health, and a policy that worsens them while not improving wellbeing is a policy with a plausible net cost. This is a single study, and the association could reflect that schools which adopt full bans are already more controlling institutions — but it is the only evidence in the set pointing to harm, and it points at the strictest configuration, which is the one jurisdictions are moving toward.

### 6. How strong is the evidence: designs, sample sizes, threats to validity, and where the reviews disagree

The evidence base is larger than it was five years ago and still structurally weak, and the reason is not laziness in the field but the nature of the intervention. Bans are adopted by whole jurisdictions at once, which destroys the comparison group a trial requires.

Ferguson makes this argument directly and it is the sharpest statement of the problem: "Unfortunately, the wide proliferation of smartphone bans without evidence may make true randomized-controlled trials unlikely at this juncture, given that it may be increasingly difficult to locate schools systematically that have not been touched by such bans" [8]. This is a specific and checkable claim about the research landscape. Once a national government legislates, there is no untreated arm left inside the country, and the study has to reach across borders into systems with different curricula, exams and cultures — which reintroduces exactly the confounding the design was meant to remove. Ferguson also states the prior plainly: "In truth, such policies have been put into place despite little evidence that such bans promote student wellbeing or grades. Indeed, several recent reviews of research in this area have shown that evidence supporting the efficacy of such bans is limited" [8].

The design quality that does exist is mostly difference-in-differences and event-study, and the best of it is candid about its limits. The most recent United States causal study uses synthetic difference-in-differences on the National Survey of Children's Health from 2016 to 2024, and states its own fragility: "Currently, there are data for only one state with two post-ban periods and two states with one post-ban period, which makes the results preliminary evidence only" [4]. That is three ban states, at most two post-treatment periods, and a finding of no clear effect on either screen time or psychological wellbeing. A synthetic control with three treated units and two post-periods cannot distinguish a null from insufficient data, and the authors say so.

The strongest counterweight to a blanket null is Abrahamsson's event study of Norwegian middle schools, and it is the single most instructive study for how to read this literature. Using administrative and survey data: "Using administrative and survey data with an event-study design, I show that banning smartphones in middle schools has no average effect on education or mental health but masks important gender differences" [6]. The heterogeneity is specific — reduced psychological health care use among girls, lower bullying for both genders, better girls' grade point averages. Two lessons follow. First, an aggregate null in a well-powered study can conceal effects in opposite directions, and the correct response to a null is to look for pre-specified subgroups rather than to conclude nothing is happening. Second, the pattern of girls being affected and boys not is repeated across independent studies in different countries, which raises its credibility above a chance finding — but it is also exactly the pattern that emerges from a hundred unrelated mechanisms, since adolescent girls report more psychological distress and use services differently at baseline.

On the quality of the underlying measures, the reviews are consistent that most studies rely on self-report and cross-sectional comparison. The consequence is a specific and serious one for a question about attention: no study in this literature measures attention with a behavioural or cognitive task. Disruptiveness is teacher- or pupil-reported conduct; attainment is exam results; wellbeing is a questionnaire. The construct that dominates the public argument is the one least directly measured.

There is one further asymmetry that a reader should hold onto. The burden of proof has been applied to bans and not to phones. A school that permits phones all day is also running an unevaluated policy, and the association evidence — consistent across countries, robust to different measures — is that more phone and social media time goes with worse sleep, more disruption and more distress. The nulls in this literature establish that school-hour prohibitions do not shift those outcomes. They do not establish that unrestricted access during the school day is fine, and the two claims are routinely confused in both directions.

One further weakness is worth naming because it affects every study here: the treatment is not stable within a jurisdiction. As the US inventory shows, state mandates cluster on bell-to-bell rules but usually leave the storage decision local — student keeps the device, classroom collection, or individual locked storage [17]. Two schools operating under the same statute can therefore deliver materially different treatments, and an evaluation that codes schools as "ban" or "no ban" will misclassify a large share of them. South Australia avoided this by specifying the hardware [12]; England's statutory guidance specifies the default but leaves enforcement to schools [10]. Where the treatment is defined by a document rather than by a practice, the measured effect is attenuated toward zero by construction, which is a reason to read the nulls as lower bounds on a well-implemented policy rather than as estimates of it.

There is also a legitimacy gradient that no study has yet modelled. Teen support falls sharply as restrictions tighten: "just 17 percent of teens supported bell-to-bell bans, compared with 41 percent of teens who supported instructional-time bans" [17]. If compliance depends on perceived legitimacy, then the effect of a ban is partly a function of how it was introduced and by whom — a national mandate imposed on hostile pupils is a different intervention from a school policy negotiated with them. The South Australian compliance figure of 87% under locked pouches [12] suggests that enforcement technology can substitute for consent, at least in the short run, but nobody has measured whether that holds over years.

The record's prior work supplies the last piece of the strength assessment, and it cuts against the mechanism the policy assumes. The screens evidence review found that the "mere presence" account of phone harm — that a device on the desk drains working memory — has largely collapsed, with a pre-registered replication failing and the largest meta-analysis finding no effect. If the harm is not from presence, it must come from use, and use is what a school-hours ban relocates rather than removes. That is the theoretical reason the nulls are not surprising, and it is why the policy question should shift from prohibition to total dose.


## Beyond this question

The finding that matters most for anyone designing or defending a policy is the dissociation between the exposure gradient and the policy effect. Every study that measures individual phone and social media use finds it associated with worse sleep, more classroom disruption and more psychological distress; no study that compares school policies finds the policy moving those outcomes. That pattern is what you would see if the harm runs through total daily dose — including the evening and the weekend — and a school-hour restriction only relocates a fraction of the dose. It implies that the policy question worth testing is not "ban or not ban" but "what reduces total exposure," and that school-hour prohibition may be a weak instrument aimed at a real target.

The second thing to carry forward is that the variation between instruments is currently being wasted. Ontario restricts use during class time with the device in the pupil's pocket; South Australia mandated bell-to-bell with magnetically locked pouches; Victoria is moving to compulsory off-and-stored with smart glasses and watches included. These are different treatments with plausibly different effect sizes, and because they were adopted at different times in different systems, they constitute a natural experiment that nobody has analysed as one. A cross-jurisdiction comparison with harmonised outcome measures would be worth more than any further single-country study.

For Chris's own work on attention, there is a specific opening. The policy debate is conducted entirely in the vocabulary of attention and focus, and the measurement is entirely about conduct. A study that put a sustained-attention or mind-wandering measure into a ban and no-ban comparison would be the first of its kind, and it would address the question policymakers believe they are answering.

## Open questions

**Nobody has measured attention.** This is the largest gap. Across the studies reviewed, attention is operationalised as reported disruptiveness, attainment or engagement. No behavioural task, no classroom observation of on-task time, no experience-sampling of mind-wandering appears in any of them. The construct that dominates the public argument is the one least directly measured.

**No post-2022 ban has been tested against exam results.** Beland and Murphy's data cover 2006–2010, before smartphone saturation; the current wave of bans has been evaluated on wellbeing, behaviour, bullying and engagement, but not on high-stakes attainment. Whether the English attainment effect survives in a school population where every pupil carries a networked device is untested.

**The Spanish bullying result needs checking against its primary source.** The 15–18% reduction is reported here as King and colleagues summarise it, not from Beneito and Vicente-Chirivella's own paper and tables. I was not able to reach the original in this pass. Until that is done, the Spanish figure should be treated as second-hand, and the tension with the Icelandic null as unresolved.

**The reconciliation between the bullying studies is my inference, not a finding.** I have suggested that recorded-incident data and pupil self-report measure different things, so a ban could reduce what schools record without reducing victimisation. Neither paper states this. It is the single most important thing to test, and the test is straightforward: collect both measures in the same schools.

**The UNESCO figure is second-hand.** The "around 40% of countries" figure comes from the 2023 Global Education Monitoring Report as cited in a 2026 Dutch study, not from the report itself. The country list it gives ("certain areas in Canada and Australia") is too coarse to be an inventory, and the report's own headline number is widely quoted in a different form. This should be replaced with the GEM Report's own text and its PEER country profiles before the figure is relied on.

**No evaluation of an Australian state ban's learning or mental health outcomes at state scale was located.** South Australia has a well-designed five-school natural experiment [12]; New South Wales, Victoria and Queensland have mandated policies but I did not find published outcome evaluations. Victoria's own instrument changed in 2026–27, which will make its early years hard to interpret. The state-level Australian evidence is therefore much thinner than the number of jurisdictions adopting bans implies.

**English evidence predates the statutory guidance.** The SMART Schools studies were conducted in 2022–23, under a regime of voluntary school policies. England's guidance became statutory on 29 June 2026, to be followed from 1 September 2026 [10]. The nulls therefore describe self-selected school policies, not a national mandate with enforcement behind it — and a mandate that changes compliance could change effects.

**A randomised trial is probably no longer possible.** Ferguson's argument that bans have spread too widely to find untreated comparison schools [8] is a structural limit on how strong this evidence can ever become. What is achievable is better quasi-experimental work across jurisdictions that adopted at different times, with pre-specified subgroups — which is essentially what Abrahamsson did, and what nobody has done across countries.

**Coverage was thin in this pass.** Both my search and page-reading allowances were exhausted before I could reach several primary documents: the Spanish bullying study, UNESCO's own report text, the NSW and Queensland education department pages, and the 2026 implementation study of South Australia's ban. One further caution on independence: several of the sources relied on here are summaries of the same underlying studies — the Icelandic, Spanish and Swedish results all reach this report through King and colleagues' review [12], and the Dutch wellbeing and bullying figures reach it through a single Springer article [14]. Where the report leans on [12] for three separate national findings, that is one review, not three independent confirmations.

**The cost-effectiveness question is unaddressed.** No study in this set compares the cost of enforcing a ban — pouches, staff time, sanctions, the disciplinary incidents generated — against the cost of an alternative use of the same resource, such as sleep education, later school start times, or a social media literacy curriculum. Given that the measured effects on wellbeing and behaviour are null and the attainment effect, where it exists, is about a week of schooling a year for the lowest achievers, the relevant policy comparison is not ban versus nothing but ban versus other things.

**Nothing here measures the effect on the pupils the policy most plausibly serves.** The South Australian data show that pupils who had experienced bullying were less likely to comply [12], which suggests the ban's costs and benefits are unevenly distributed in ways no study has estimated. Whether a phone-free school day helps the pupil who is being harassed on a platform at night, or merely removes their means of reaching support during the day, is unmeasured.

**I could not check the 2024 rapid review or the health-economics analysis.** Both were identified as directly relevant; the review's publisher page refused access on the second attempt and the health-economics paper returned 403. Their conclusions are therefore absent from §6 rather than summarised, and this is a real gap in the strength assessment rather than an omission by choice. Reply "keep going" and I will fetch the missing primaries and revise.

sentences.sentence: Stated in the form the Library and Archives Canada exposition of the Innis–McLuhan collection gives them, the analyst asks what a medium extends or enhances, what it obsolesces or pushes out of the picture, what earlier thing it retrieves that had previously been obsolesced [1][3], and what it flips or reverses into when pushed to the limit of its potential.

Whether the answers form a determinate pattern for a given artefact is the question the whole subsequent literature turns on, and the McLuhans' own practice on wine suggests they do not: two different tetrads for the same object appear on a single page of *Laws of Media* [2].
The archive exposition is explicit that the four exist at once and that although McLuhan sometimes talked about them as succeeding each other, he did not intend them to be read chronologically [1].

In McLuhan's late vocabulary, the "ground" of any technology is twofold: the situation that gives rise to it, and the whole environment of services and disservices the technology brings with it, which impose themselves "willy-nilly as a new form of culture" [3].

The archive text puts the methodological requirement plainly: to grasp the impact of a new technology one must examine figure and ground together, "since neither is comprehensible without the other" [3].
The four laws "further exhibit McLuhan's abiding concern with pedagogy: they are meant to be used as tools to analyze the patterns of effects that different technologies produce" [1].

The archive exposition goes further: the tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool but one for exploring the grammar and syntax of each artefact, a dynamic instrument for describing situations that are in process [1].

That gap between the kind of claim made and the kind of test available is why the empirical question has been answered in the negative rather than by experiment: the verdict of the critical literature is that the tetrad is unfalsifiable, not that it was falsified [2].

Tyler's reading of that paper and its 1977 successor in *et cetera* is that McLuhan asserted the four laws were testable hypotheses, and a "scientific method" modelled on Popper's principle of falsifiability [2].
Henry Venable titled "Flaws in McLuhan's Laws" — volume 17, issue 2, April 1976, page 256 — and McLuhan replied in the same journal in a piece called "Misunderstanding the Media's Laws" [9].

Eric McLuhan's formulation in *Laws of Media* — that the four questions "can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" [2] — is a universal reproducibility claim of exactly the kind Popperian falsification requires.
Tyler's response to it is one sentence: "This is not, in fact, the case" [2].

McLuhan's prose makes ordinary scholarly building difficult: he used deliberately multi-vocal language, in Meyrowitz's description the "textured oral language of puns and poetry—where words intentionally have more than one meaning—to make the arguments of science" [8], and his books lacked indexes, citation footnotes and cumulative structure.
Nystrom's founding definition, reprinted alongside it, describes the field as "a preparadigmatic science" [7].

It has been in fields that needed a quick, teachable, four-box structure for thinking about a new tool, and that found in McLuhan a licence to ask about effects rather than content. **Software testing and organisational design.** Michael Bolton, a software testing consultant, published "McLuhan for Testers" in *Better Software* in October 2007, presenting the four laws as four probes — he calls them "testing heuristics" — that can be applied to a requirement, a feature, a test approach or an organisational change [4].
He frames the payoff as anticipating and managing reversal effects [4].

This is the tetrad functioning as a risk register with four fixed columns. **Health services.** Ganiem (2020), in the Indonesian journal *Interaksi*, applied the tetrad to telemedicine as "healing at a distance," using a qualitative descriptive review of 23 international journals published between 2015 and 2020, and structuring the entire analysis around enhancement, obsolescence, reversal and retrieval [6].

This is the standard form the tetrad takes when it travels: a sorting device applied to secondary literature. **Pedagogy and the generic template.** A 2016 essay in the undergraduate journal *Glocality* applies the tetrad to the smartphone, opening with the claim that McLuhan "developed a scientific model summing up his ideas, the tetrad", which "is applicable as a tool of analysis to any technology or artefact" [5].

His methodological innovations — defining obsolescence as remediation rather than extinction, reporting where the evidence is "collectively uncertain," declining to build "potentially Procrustean taxonomies of play" — are the closest thing in the literature to a set of quality standards for a tetrad analysis [2]. **Design and HCI.** The tetrad circulates in design and human-computer interaction as a lightweight futures tool, usually paired with figure/ground analysis.
That is a legitimate use, and it is the use McLuhan's own curators endorsed [1].

A 2001 cross-European media-use study found that electronic games had taken the third position behind television and audio media, a position previously held by print, at least among boys; but the authors warned that their cross-sectional data was "unfit to determine causal relationships" between different kinds of media [2].

He then adds Nick Yee's Daedalus Project figures: MMORPG players averaged 21.0 hours per week playing and 7.7 hours per week watching television, which sums to roughly the national television average of 28, and Yee offered this as support for displacement [2].
Tyler's verdict on the whole body of evidence is that none of these studies is conclusive [2].
Meyrowitz's verdict is that McLuhan's contribution was generative rather than substantive, inspirational rather than instructional [8].

Christine Nystrom's founding definition of media ecology, written in 1973 and still reproduced by the Media Ecology Association as one of three canonical statements of what the field is, called it "a preparadigmatic science" [7] — a field that knows what it is interested in but does not yet have a coherent framework in which to organise its subject matter or its questions.
Tyler notes that McLuhan always urged that one should never predict anything that has not already happened [2], and that the four laws operate simultaneously rather than in sequence.

I found no inter-coder reliability study, no pre-registered application, and no published attempt to identify a case in which a quadrant failed — though a corpus of McLuhan's own submitted tetrads is now in print and would support such a study [10].

If such a study exists, it is not indexed where a search for it would find it, which is itself evidence about the state of the field. **The corpus that could settle the reliability question.** The most useful thing I found, and the least used, is that a body of McLuhan's own tetrad submissions has been published: *The Lost Tetrads of Marshall McLuhan* (OR Books) contains a chapter on tetrad development and examples of submissions running from page 11 to page 40 [10].

Conceived as a universal scientific method, he writes, "the tetrad is far too vague: a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any human artefact, a huge range of things which it might be considered to augment, obsolesce, retrieve, and reverse into" [2].
The laws, he adds, "do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all, since empirical examples can readily be stretched to fit" [2].
Like Procrustes' bed, the tetrad is "unrelentingly rigid: it requires us to fill the gaps" [2].

Tyler asks whether we really want to say that wine obsolesces commonplace flavours or retrieves ritual observance, and answers that forcing these complex notions into the tetrad's frame does them violence [2].

notes.claim: Tom Tyler's (Oxford Brookes) DiGRA 2007 paper is the sharpest post-1988 statement of the unfalsifiability charge: because a creative analyst can generate a vast range of candidate answers for any artefact, empirical examples can always be stretched to fit, so the tetrad cannot be falsified.

notes.quote: At the same time, just like Procrustes’ bed, McLuhan’s tetrad is unrelentingly rigid: it requires us to fill the gaps. Do we really wish to suggest that wine obsolesces “commonplace flavours” or that it retrieves “ritual observance”? Perhaps, but we do violence to these complex notions when they are hewn to fit the tetrad’s frame.
notes.claim: The Procrustean-rigidity objection: the tetrad is not only too loose but simultaneously too rigid, since it compels the analyst to fill all four quadrants whether or not the evidence supports it, doing violence to the phenomena. Tyler's framing is a double bind, not a single charge of vagueness.

notes.quote: the ground of any technology is both the situation that gives rise to it as well as the whole environment (medium) of services and disservices that the technology brings with it. These are side-effects and impose themselves willy-nilly as a new form of culture.
notes.claim: The tetrad's derivation from figure/ground: the ground of a technology is the situation that gives rise to it plus the whole environment of services and disservices it brings; effects are side-effects imposed willy-nilly.

notes.quote: To fully grasp the impact a new technology will have, one must examine figure and ground together, since neither is comprehensible without the other.
notes.claim: Figure and ground must be examined together for the tetrad's four effects to be grasped — the tetrad operationalises the figure/ground pairing.

notes.quote: When faced with a requirement to evaluate, a feature to test, a test approach, or an organizational change, the Laws of Media might help you notice what might be extended, retrieved, and obsolesced— and how you might anticipate and manage some of the reversal effects.
notes.claim: Bolton frames the tetrad as a practical tool for organisational change and management, not just media analysis — anticipating reversal effects when introducing something like a dedicated test team.

notes.quote: At a later stage of his life, McLuhan developed a scientific model summing up his ideas, the tetrad. It is applicable as a tool of analysis to any technology or artefact, which will be done with the smartphone in the course of this essay.
notes.claim: A peer-reviewed undergraduate journal essay (Glocality, 2016) applies the tetrad to the smartphone as a demonstration that the tetrad is "applicable as a tool of analysis to any technology or artefact" — an example of the tetrad's use as a generic pedagogical/analytical template.

This research method uses a qualitative descriptive by reviewing 23 relevant international journals discussing telemedicine, tetrad, or health services published from 2015-2020.

notes.quote: McLuhan believed that the tetrad provides “an ordering of thought and experience” [19], and it is my argument that ordering our thinking and experience of key aspects of digital gameplay by means of his probe allows us both to situate that play within the broader media environment
notes.claim: Tyler's own summary of what the tetrad contributes even after conceding it is not science: it provides an ordering of thought and experience, a systematic way of organising existing insights about a technology.

notes.quote: Their findings suggest that “electronic games have conquered the third position behind television and audio media” previously held by print [4], at least amongst boys, though the impact on television viewing is unclear, and the authors warn that the cross-sectional data they present is “unfit to determine causal relationships” between different kinds of media [4].

In other words, this lends support to the claim that time that was spent watching TV has been displaced by MMORPG playing” [37]. None of these studies is by any means conclusive.
notes.claim: The single quantitative datum Tyler uses to support the obsolescence quadrant: Nick Yee's Daedalus Project figures showing MMORPG players average 21.0 hours per week gaming and 7.7 hours watching TV, summing to roughly the national TV average of 28 — offered as support for displacement, though Tyler calls none of these studies conclusive.

notes.quote: The question seems to invite wild speculation regarding future developments, but McLuhan himself always urged that one should “Never predict anything that hasn’t already happened” [quoted in 10].
notes.claim: McLuhan's own injunction against prediction, quoted by Tyler: the reversal law is not futurology because it concerns potentials already present. Tyler uses this to argue reversal should be read as what has already begun to happen.

notes.quote: Media ecology is, in short, a preparadigmatic science.
notes.claim: Christine Nystrom's 1973 doctoral dissertation, reprinted by the Media Ecology Association as a canonical definition, characterised media ecology as "a preparadigmatic science" without a coherent framework — a founding self-description of the field that inherited the tetrad.

notes.quote: But he did not tell us how one goes about studying things such as a “shifting sensorium” or what types of behavioral changes to look for. How, for example, does one further study people who, in McLuhan’s view, “live mythically and integrally”? What evidence can we gather to test, support, or disprove his claims? In short, McLuhan’s contribution has been generative, rather than substantive, inspirational rather than instructional.
notes.claim: Joshua Meyrowitz, in his 2001 MEA keynote, states the methodological gap precisely: McLuhan gave a battle cry and a general direction but never said how to study a shifting sensorium or what evidence could test, support or disprove his claims. His verdict is that McLuhan's contribution has been generative rather than substantive.

notes.quote: Instead, he attempted to use the textured oral language of puns and poetry—where words intentionally have more than one meaning—to make the arguments of science.
notes.claim: Meyrowitz on why McLuhan's prose resists ordinary scholarly extension: he used deliberately multi-vocal poetic language to make the arguments of science, rather than defining terms precisely.

notes.quote: The idea that these are “scientific laws” in anything like the sense in which we ordinarily use the term is preposterous. And yet the tetrad has its uses.
notes.claim: Tyler occupies precisely the middle ground the section says is nearly unavailable: the tetrad is worthless as science yet valuable as an exploratory probe, so the post-1988 literature does not simply divide into "genuine discovery" versus "template".

notes.quote: The laws of media do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all, since empirical examples can readily be stretched to fit.
notes.claim: The testability of the tetrad has in fact been addressed directly and given a clear verdict: it is not falsifiable, because examples can always be stretched to fit. The empirical question has been answered, not left dangling for want of an appropriate test.

notes.quote: Or, at least, these are the answers the first time they apply the tetrad. In an alternative version on the same page, we find that wine enhances food and “the occasion”, obsolesces “inhibition”, retrieves “festive spontaneity of speech and gesture”, and reverses into “hangover” and insult.
notes.claim: The McLuhans' own book gives two different, incompatible tetrads for the same artefact (wine) on a single page, so the answers do not in fact come in a fixed pattern even in the authors' own hands.

notes.claim: Eric McLuhan's claim in Laws of Media that the tetrad's answers can be asked and checked by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact — a reproducibility/checkability claim that bears directly on whether the tetrad is testable, and which the section omits.
