sentences.sentence: This is the standard reading in the literature and the only one that could be shown wrong in a useful way. **Second, which measure.** Statistics Canada defines the employment rate as the "Number of employed persons expressed as a percentage of the population 15 years of age and older" [3], so a fall in the youth employment rate can be produced by fewer jobs, by more young people in school, or by a larger youth population.
Employment itself is measured generously: employed persons are those who "did any work for pay or profit or had a job and were absent from work" in the reference week [3].

Statistics Canada collects labour-market information from age 15 up [3], and the Canadian literature conventionally reports teenagers (15–19) separately from youth (15–24) because the results differ sharply between them.

Statistics Canada's own survey article states the established Canadian pattern plainly: "small or non-existent" effects on total employment, and a decrease "associated with a decrease in employment among teenagers" [4].

Statistics Canada makes the point directly: "These effects do not necessarily take the form of layoffs, but may instead take the form of reduced hiring, which diminishes the job prospects of teenagers." [4] Evidence that separations did not rise, or that no firm cut its existing workforce, is therefore not a refutation.

It applies meta-regression methods to test for publication bias and to recover an effect size after adjusting for it, and for the group that matters it reports: "For teenagers, the demographic group with the largest share of minimum wage workers and thus providing the findings of most interest to policy-makers and legislators, I find no evidence of a publication bias" [5].

The paper's teenage estimate is a minimum-wage elasticity of about −0.27 [5] — on its face, a 10% rise in the floor associated with roughly a 2.7% fall in teenage employment (my arithmetic from the elasticity, not a figure the paper states).

They find that minimum-wage increases raised the transition out of employment for at-risk low-wage youths "by around 6 percentage points (ranging from 4 to 8 percentage points)", which implies elasticities of about −0.4 [6].

This is a better-identified design than a cross-province employment-rate regression, because it follows the same individuals and asks whether the ones exposed to the new floor left work more often than the ones who were not. **The panel evidence on employment rates is consistent in sign.** Rybczynski and Sen (2018) assemble the full provincial record: "This paper studies the effects of 185 amendments to minimum wage on employment rates using panel data across Canadian provinces from 1981 to 2011." [7] Using both ordinary least squares and instrumental variables, they find that a 10% increase in the minimum wage is associated with a 1% to 4% reduction in teen employment rates, for male and female teens alike [7].
For 1983–2000 there is no statistically significant effect on employment growth, but for 2001–2016 there is a statistically significant negative effect [8].

If the effect only became detectable once minimum wages began rising faster relative to prevailing wages, then the much larger increases after 2017 are exactly where the effect should be most visible, not least. **Exposure is concentrated where the thesis says it is, and steeply so by age.** In 2013, "61% of minimum wage employees were aged 15 to 24" [4] — up from 57% in 1997 — and the share of employees paid at the minimum wage falls off sharply with age: "In 2013, 50% of employees aged 15 to 19 and 13% of those aged 20 to 24 were paid at minimum wage" [4], against 3.5% of 25-to-34-year-olds and 2.8% of those aged 35 to 64 [4].
This is why the Canadian literature's own summary is not a null: it reports effects on total employment that would "typically be small or non-existent" alongside a decrease among teenagers [4].

According to Fortin (2010), when the ratio is close to 50%, the effects on the employment of teenagers are relatively significant." [4] In 2013, before the wave of increases, that ratio stood at between 42% and 49% depending on the earnings measure used [4], and the article traces a rise in the ratio from 2005 to 2013 after a decline from 1997 to 2005 [4].

That is the strongest form of the case for. **The mechanism is hiring, not firing — which is why the thesis survives the obvious rebuttal.** Statistics Canada states the mechanism explicitly: "These effects do not necessarily take the form of layoffs, but may instead take the form of reduced hiring, which diminishes the job prospects of teenagers." [4] And in the summary of Brochu and Green (2012): "when the minimum wage is high, labour market transitions (hirings and layoffs) tend to decrease", with the reduction in hirings for teenagers exceeding the reduction in layoffs, producing a significant negative employment effect, while for older workers the two roughly cancel [4].

While the net impact on labour income would be positive, employment would fall by 60,000—a number that lies in the lower part of a range obtained from an accounting exercise (30,000 to 140,000)." [10] This is the closest thing to an official Canadian estimate of the post-2017 episode, and it is a *projection* built on pre-existing elasticities, not an ex-post measurement — which is both its use and its limit for the thesis.

It does not show that one occurred. **And there is a sectoral signal in the right place.** In the twelve months to May 2019 — the window covering Ontario's January 2018 increase and Alberta's completion of its climb — Statistics Canada reported that accommodation and food services employment "has trended downward since May 2018, decreasing by 63,000 (\-5.0%) over the 12 months" [11].

The Fraser Institute's Philip Cross states the pro-thesis position at its strongest when he writes that "There is near unanimity among researchers that higher minimum wages cause employment losses in Canada, especially among youths who account for most of the people earning a minimum wage." [9] But a claim of near-unanimity about incremental increases is not evidence about a step change of the size several provinces legislated after 2017.

They exploit "rich Canadian data consisting of a large set of short panels (and covering a period with over 150 changes in nominal minimum wages)" to decompose what happens to the wage distribution at the moment a minimum wage rises, separating job leavers, job joiners and workers who stay put [2].

The paper reports: "We find that minimum wage increases do not result in an abnormal concentration of Job Leavers below the new minimum wage, which is inconsistent with employment effects predicted by a neoclassical model." [1] On the leaver margin specifically: "When we implement our estimator for Job Leavers, we find no effect of upcoming minimum wage changes." [2] And they read the pattern as decisive against the textbook channel: "Thus, this result (plus the existence of a spike at the minimum wage) rejects standard neoclassical models and is potentially problematic for other models as well." [2] They do not claim to have settled whether employment falls at all.

The paper states that "there is still some debate on the existence and size of employment effects" and that it is designed to be robust to that debate, and it describes its own contribution as showing the effects of minimum wages on the shape of the wage distribution in order to discriminate between models of the labour market [2].

It is a study of the shape of the wage distribution, not an employment-effects study; the authors note that the Cengiz-style estimator "is ideally constructed to answer questions about shifts in employment related to a minimum wage change" [2], which is a different question from the one they answer.
The data period runs "from January 1997 through December 2016" [2], so the paper contains no observations from the 2017-onward window at all.
And the estimation sample excludes full-time students, because in the authors' words "working is not their main activity" [2] — yet students are a large share of the teenagers the thesis is about.

It is not a test of the 2017 episode, and it is not a test of the students who make up much of the youth minimum-wage workforce. **The timing result.** The same paper finds the wage structure adjusts quickly: "We find no evidence of dynamics beyond about 2 months after a minimum wage increase." [2] This is a finding about wages, not about employment — the paper does not estimate employment dynamics — so it cannot by itself date any employment response.
Statistics Canada's employment rate divides the employed by the whole population of the group [3], so the rate moves with the size of the youth population as well as with the number of jobs.

In May 2019, employment among 17-to-19-year-old students was up 35,000, or 8.5%, over the year, and yet "The employment rate was little changed at 50.7%, as the population of students in this age group grew at a similar pace to employment." [11] Jobs rose and the rate did not, because the denominator rose with them.

Any study that reads a flat or falling youth employment rate after 2017 as evidence of fewer jobs has to net out that population growth first, and the studies in the case for do not do so for this window. **The aggregate picture in the pre-pandemic window is hard to reconcile with a large effect.** By May 2019, after Ontario's January 2018 increase and Alberta's completion of its climb to a $15 floor, Statistics Canada reported that "The unemployment rate in May was the lowest since comparable data became available in 1976." [11] Youth employment was up 64,000, or 2.6%, over the year [11].

The minimum-wage literature's standard identification — comparing provinces with bigger increases to provinces with smaller ones — is also compromised in this window, because the pandemic hit provinces unequally (Ontario and Quebec, the two largest, had the longest and strictest closures) and because the federal wage subsidy removed the usual link between labour cost and employment for much of 2020–21. **Provincial timing does not line up the way the thesis needs.** The Bank of Canada note that assessed this episode describes it as a set of "scheduled minimum wage increases over the coming years" [10] — that is, a programme legislated province by province with different magnitudes and different start dates, which is what makes a cross-province comparison possible in principle.

Where teen employment did fall sharply — 2020 — it fell everywhere at once, which is the signature of a common shock rather than a provincial policy difference. **The wider literature is also drifting toward smaller effects — though the comparison is imperfect for Canada.** Wolfson and Belman's meta-analysis of 37 US studies published since the Card–Krueger–Neumark–Wascher exchange of December 2000 finds that the consensus range has moved toward zero, from an interval of −0.3 to −0.1 to one of −0.13 to −0.07, and concludes that "The minimum wage has negative employment effects, but these have become notably smaller and are largely localized to teenagers." [12] That challenges the premise that effects are large and stable enough to have produced a visible national fall in youth employment after 2017.
It is, however, a US result, and Statistics Canada is explicit that the Canadian teenage effect is larger than the American one [4], so it should not be transplanted wholesale.

Its use here is narrower: it shows that the direction of travel in the best-studied labour market is toward smaller, teen-only effects, which makes a large post-2017 Canadian effect less likely, not impossible. **What the case against does not establish.** The paper does report results for new job joiners as well as leavers — "For completeness, we also present the results for new job Joiners." [2] — but the leaver null cannot carry the weight of refuting the thesis on its own, and the authors supply the reason themselves: "A possible explanation for these findings is that firms do not layoff additional workers in response to a minimum wage increase, but reduce hiring to keep employment constant since workers are now less likely to quit." [2] A thesis about young people failing to get jobs is not refuted by a finding that existing workers kept theirs.

Statistics Canada's summary of the Canadian evidence says the adjustment runs through hiring: hirings and layoffs both fall when the minimum wage is high, and for teenagers the fall in hirings exceeds the fall in layoffs, which is what produces the negative employment effect, whereas for older workers the two cancel [4].

Brochu, Green, Lemieux and Townsend (NBER Working Paper 33479, 2025) build that test on "rich Canadian data consisting of a large set of short panels (and covering a period with over 150 changes in nominal minimum wages)", decomposing what happens to the wage distribution at the time of an increase into job leavers, joiners and continuing workers [2].

Their leaver result is a clean null: "We find that minimum wage increases do not result in an abnormal concentration of Job Leavers below the new minimum wage, which is inconsistent with employment effects predicted by a neoclassical model." [1] The authors read their own result as decisive against the textbook channel — the absence of a leaver spike alongside a spike in the wage distribution "rejects standard neoclassical models and is potentially problematic for other models as well" [2] — but they are careful about what they have not done.

They describe their contribution as showing the effects of minimum wages on the overall shape of the wage distribution in order to discriminate between models of the labour market [2], and they note that a different estimator, the one associated with Cengiz and co-authors, "is ideally constructed to answer questions about shifts in employment related to a minimum wage change" [2].

In other words, the paper that most directly tests the mechanism is not itself an employment-effects study. **Why the leaver test does not settle the thesis.** The authors supply the reason in their own discussion: "A possible explanation for these findings is that firms do not layoff additional workers in response to a minimum wage increase, but reduce hiring to keep employment constant since workers are now less likely to quit." [2] A hiring-driven effect would produce exactly the pattern they report — no abnormal concentration of leavers, and a wage distribution that shifts upward within about two months [2].
Its data period runs "from January 1997 through December 2016" [2], so it contains no observations from the window the thesis names.

And the estimation sample excludes full-time students [2], who are a large share of the young workers at the minimum wage. **The second crux: whether the post-2017 increases were inside or outside the range the literature covers.** The case for rests on estimates of roughly −0.27 for teenagers from a meta-analysis of the Canadian literature with no detected publication bias [5], about −0.4 from a longitudinal transitions study of the 1990s [6], and 1–4% teen employment-rate reductions per 10% minimum-wage increase from a panel of 185 provincial amendments between 1981 and 2011 [7].

According to Fortin (2010), when the ratio is close to 50%, the effects on the employment of teenagers are relatively significant." [4] In 2013 that ratio was between 42% and 49% depending on the earnings measure [4], and it had been rising since 2005 after falling from 1997 to 2005 [4].

So the crux is not whether the teenage elasticity is −0.27 or zero; it is where on the ratio that elasticity changes, and no Canadian study I found estimates that schedule for the levels reached after 2017. **A related caution: the Canadian effect is not the US effect, and US evidence should not be substituted.** Statistics Canada states it directly — "The negative effect on employment is higher in Canada than in the United States." [4] That cuts both ways for the thesis.

It also means the shrinking US estimates reported by Wolfson and Belman [12] are weaker counter-evidence than they first appear, because the institutional baseline they describe is not Canada's. **A third crux the literature rarely states: what "employment" is being measured.** The Canadian studies summarised above mostly measure employment as a headcount or an employment rate.

If the true adjustment in the post-2017 episode ran through hours rather than headcount, every study in this debate — on both sides — would understate the effect, and the thesis would be simultaneously true in spirit and unprovable with the measures in use. **What the crux shows so far.** The literature has (a) a consistent, bias-corrected finding that Canadian minimum wages reduce teenage employment by a modest amount, estimated mostly on pre-2017 variation; (b) one strong, recent Canadian test that finds no evidence of the job-destruction channel, on data ending in 2016 and excluding students; (c) an official projection from the Bank of Canada in December 2017 that the scheduled increases would cost about 60,000 jobs by early 2019 [10]; and (d) no study that estimates the effect of the specific 2017-onward provincial increases on youth employment with a design that separates them from the pandemic.

The nearest official assessment is the Bank of Canada's December 2017 projection of about 60,000 jobs lost by early 2019 [10], which is a simulation of the scheduled increases, not a measurement of what they did.
Statistics Canada's summary of the Canadian literature says the effect runs through hirings [4], so the data to test it should exist.
The Canadian paper that comes closest reports joiner results alongside leaver results [2] but does not present them as an employment-effects estimate for the post-2017 period.

According to Fortin (2010), when the ratio is close to 50%, the effects on the employment of teenagers are relatively significant." [4] In 2013 that ratio was between 42% and 49% depending on the measure [4].

Statistics Canada's own releases show the denominator moving materially in this window — employment among 17-to-19-year-old students rose 8.5% while the employment rate stayed at 50.7% because the student population grew just as fast [11].
Brochu, Green, Lemieux and Townsend find no abnormal concentration of job leavers below the new minimum wage and no effect of upcoming minimum wage changes on leavers [1][2].
It does not end it, because the thesis can be true through reduced hiring, and the authors themselves offer that as the explanation for their null [2].

That requires the difference-in-differences described above, estimated with enough precision to rule out an effect the size the meta-analysis reports — roughly a 2.7% fall in teenage employment per 10% rise in the floor, if the elasticity of about −0.27 is taken at face value [5].

Wolfson and Belman's meta-analysis of 37 US studies published since 2000 finds the consensus range has shifted from −0.3 to −0.1 toward −0.13 to −0.07, with effects "largely localized to teenagers" [12].

notes.quote: We find that minimum wage increases do not result in an abnormal concentration of Job Leavers below the new minimum wage, which is inconsistent with employment effects predicted by a neoclassical model.
notes.claim: The most direct test of the mechanism that would have to generate youth job losses — layoffs/separations concentrating among workers paid just below the new minimum — comes back negative in Canadian data. This is the evidence that would overturn the thesis if it went the other way, and it does not.

notes.quote: When we implement our estimator for Job Leavers, we find no effect of upcoming minimum wage changes.
notes.claim: Brochu, Green, Lemieux and Townsend (NBER WP 33479, Feb 2025) find no change in the wage distribution of job leavers at the time of a Canadian minimum wage increase — the test the "reduced employment" thesis needs to pass.

notes.quote: **Employment rate (employment/population ratio):** Number of employed persons expressed as a percentage of the population 15 years of age and older. The employment rate for a particular group (for example, one defined by age, gender, or province) is the number employed in that group expressed as a percentage of the population for that group.
notes.claim: Statistics Canada's official definition: the employment rate divides employed persons by the whole population of the group, not by the labour force. So "reduced employment among young workers" can mean a lower employment rate (which also moves with school enrolment and population change) or a lower number employed — two different claims.

notes.quote: **Employment:** Employed persons are those who, during the reference week, did any work for pay or profit or had a job and were absent from work.
notes.claim: Employment is measured as any work at all in the reference week — one hour counts as employed. A minimum-wage-induced cut in hours (e.g. from 30 to 12 hours a week) would not show up as reduced employment on this measure, so the thesis must specify whether it is about headcount or hours.

notes.quote: **Age:** Age is collected for every household member in the survey, and the information on labour market activity is collected for all persons aged 15 and older.
notes.claim: The LFS collects labour market data from age 15 up, and "youth" is conventionally the 15-24 group while "teenagers" is 15-19 — so the thesis's "young workers" needs an age band specified, because the Canadian literature finds effects concentrated among teens and absent for 20-24 year-olds.

notes.quote: In Canada, the effects of an increase in the minimum wage on total employment would typically be small or non-existent.Note 2 Rather, an increase in the minimum wage would seem to be associated with a decrease in employment among teenagers,Note 3 who are most likely to be paid at this hourly rate.
notes.claim: Statistics Canada's own survey article states the established Canadian finding: effects on total employment are small or nil, and the negative effect is concentrated on teenagers. This is the scope the thesis must adopt to be defensible — it is a claim about teens/young workers specifically, not about employment overall.

notes.quote: These effects do not necessarily take the form of layoffs, but may instead take the form of reduced hiring, which diminishes the job prospects of teenagers.
notes.claim: The mechanism matters for what the thesis claims: reduced employment need not mean layoffs, but reduced hiring. A finding of "no layoffs" therefore does not refute the thesis, and a finding of fewer jobs for young people does not require any employer to have fired anyone.

notes.quote: According to Brochu and Green (2012), when the minimum wage is high, labour market transitions (hirings and layoffs) tend to decrease. For teenagers, the reductions in hirings largely exceed the number of layoffs, which explains why there is a significant and negative effect on employment in this age group. For older workers, the reduction in layoffs largely offsets the reduction in hirings, with a nil or insignificant effect on employment.
notes.claim: Statistics Canada summarises Brochu and Green (2012): for teenagers the fall in hiring far exceeds layoffs, giving a significant negative employment effect; for older workers reduced layoffs offset reduced hiring, giving a nil effect. This is why age-disaggregation is the crux of the thesis, not an optional refinement.

notes.quote: Hence, 61% of minimum wage employees were aged 15 to 24 in 2013 (57% in 1997).
notes.claim: Establishes the exposure: 61% of minimum-wage employees in Canada were aged 15-24, and 50.2% of employees aged 15-19 were paid at the minimum wage in 2013. Any effect of a minimum-wage rise has to show up disproportionately among young workers for the thesis to be plausible.

notes.quote: For teenagers, the demographic group with the largest share of minimum wage workers and thus providing the findings of most interest to policy-makers and legislators, I find no evidence of a publication bias
notes.claim: Campolieti's 2020 meta-analysis of the Canadian literature reports no publication bias for teenagers and a teenage employment elasticity of about −0.27 (minus 0.27), the best single summary estimate of the pre-2017 Canadian literature.

notes.quote: by around 6 percentage points (ranging from 4 to 8 percentage points)
notes.claim: Campolieti, Fang and Gunderson (2005), using SLID longitudinal data and 24 provincial minimum wage changes in the 1990s, find low-wage youths' employment-to-non-employment transitions rise by about 6 percentage points (4 to 8), implying minimum wage elasticities of about −0.4 (−0.3 to −0.5).

notes.quote: This paper studies the effects of 185 amendments to minimum wage on employment rates using panel data across Canadian provinces from 1981 to 2011.
notes.claim: Rybczynski and Sen (2018) use 185 provincial minimum wage amendments from 1981 to 2011 with OLS and IV and find a 10% minimum wage increase associated with a 1% to 4% reduction in teen employment rates, for both male and female teens.
