notes.claim: Campolieti (2018) finds no statistically significant effect on restaurant-sector employment growth in 1983–2000 but a statistically significant negative effect for 2001–2016 — the effect is period-dependent, and stronger in the recent period.

notes.quote: using rich Canadian data consisting of a large set of short panels (and covering a period with over 150 changes in nominal minimum wages), we are able to decompose the effects of a change in the minimum wage on the wage distribution into elements related to job turnover and wage changes for continuing workers
notes.claim: Brochu, Green, Lemieux and Townsend use Canadian data covering a period with more than 150 changes in nominal minimum wages, decomposing wage-distribution effects into leavers, joiners and stayers.

notes.quote: Thus, this result (plus the existence of a spike at the minimum wage) rejects standard neoclassical models and is potentially problematic for other models as well.
notes.claim: The authors state their no-effect-on-leavers finding rejects standard neoclassical models, and they note it fits with results implying small employment impacts, citing Cengiz et al. and Brochu and Green (2013).

notes.quote: We find no evidence of dynamics beyond about 2 months after a minimum wage increase.
notes.claim: The authors find the wage structure adjusts within about two months of a minimum wage change — relevant to whether effects would appear quickly in employment data.

notes.quote: There is near unanimity among researchers that higher minimum wages cause employment losses in Canada, especially among youths who account for most of the people earning a minimum wage.
notes.claim: Philip Cross's Fraser Institute study (March 2021) asserts near unanimity that higher minimum wages cause employment losses in Canada, especially among youths, but concedes the extent varies and that Canada has little experience with increases as large as Alberta's and Ontario's — i.e. the large-increase case is extrapolated from incremental-increase evidence.

notes.quote: A possible explanation for these findings is that firms do not layoff additional workers in response to a minimum wage increase, but reduce hiring to keep employment constant since workers are now less likely to quit.
notes.claim: The authors themselves say the null result on the leavers margin is compatible with firms cutting hiring instead of laying off incumbents — i.e. employment could fall through the entry margin, which is exactly the channel a "reduced employment among young workers" thesis needs. So the leaver null is not decisive against the thesis.

notes.quote: For our main estimates, we work with the data at the monthly level, with our data period running from January 1997 through December 2016.
notes.claim: The study's sample ends in December 2016, so it contains no observations from the 2017-onward window the thesis is about.

notes.quote: We further exclude full-time students because working is not their main activity.
notes.claim: Full-time students are excluded from the estimation sample, so the paper's null says nothing about the student teenagers who make up much of the youth minimum-wage workforce.

notes.quote: For completeness, we also present the results for new job Joiners.
notes.claim: The paper does estimate effects for job Joiners (Section 6.4.3, Figure 13, and the Joiners columns of Tables 1 and 3), contrary to the claim that the authors test leavers but not joiners.

notes.quote: Given that there is still some debate on the existence and size of employment effects, we believe it is better to use an estimator that is robust to their existence.
notes.claim: The authors do not claim to have settled whether minimum wages reduce employment; they explicitly design around the continuing debate on the existence and size of employment effects.

notes.quote: Our main contribution is to show the effects of minimum wages on the overall shape of the wage distribution and to use that to differentiate between different models of the labour market.
notes.claim: The paper's stated aim is to discriminate between models of the labour market, not to estimate employment effects; its results are offered as patterns for others to use.

notes.quote: A structural general equilibrium simulation suggests that minimum wage increases would reduce the level of gross domestic product by roughly 0.1 per cent by early 2019 and boost CPI inflation by about 0.1 pp. While the net impact on labour income would be positive, employment would fall by 60,000—a number that lies in the lower part of a range obtained from an accounting exercise (30,000 to 140,000).
notes.claim: The Bank of Canada's December 2017 staff analytical note on the scheduled provincial minimum wage increases projects, from a structural general equilibrium simulation, that employment would fall by 60,000 by early 2019 — the lower part of a 30,000 to 140,000 range from an accounting exercise — and that GDP would be about 0.1 per cent lower. This is the closest thing to an official Canadian estimate of the post-2017 increases, and it is a projection, not an ex-post measurement.

notes.quote: The unemployment rate in May was the lowest since comparable data became available in 1976.
notes.claim: By May 2019 — after Ontario's January 2018 increase and Alberta's completion of its climb to $15 — the national unemployment rate was the lowest since comparable data began in 1976 (5.4%), and youth employment was up 64,000 (+2.6%) year over year. This is aggregate context, not a causal test, but it constrains how large any youth disemployment effect could have been.

notes.quote: Employment in this industry has trended downward since May 2018, decreasing by 63,000 (\-5.0%) over the 12 months.
notes.claim: In the same release, employment in accommodation and food services — the industry most exposed to minimum wages — had trended downward since May 2018 and fell 63,000 (-5.0%) over the 12 months to May 2019, the period covering the largest provincial increases. This is consistent with a sectoral effect but equally with other shocks, and the release offers no causal attribution.

notes.quote: from January 1997 through December 2016
notes.claim: The Brochu–Green–Lemieux–Townsend sample runs from January 1997 through December 2016, so it contains no post-2017 observations and cannot directly test the thesis's period.

notes.quote: We further exclude full-time students because working is not their main activity
notes.claim: The study excludes full-time students from its sample, so its findings do not cover the student teenagers who make up a large share of minimum-wage workers.

notes.quote: firms do not layoff additional workers in response to a minimum wage increase, but reduce hiring to keep employment constant since workers are now less likely to quit
notes.claim: The authors themselves explain how reduced hiring, not layoffs, would follow a minimum wage rise: firms do not lay off extra workers but reduce hiring to keep employment constant, since workers are now less likely to quit. This means a leaver null does not exhaust the thesis's mechanism.

notes.quote: is ideally constructed to answer questions about shifts in employment related to a minimum wage change
notes.claim: The paper says its own estimator is designed to show effects on the overall shape of the wage distribution, while the Cengiz et al. estimator is the one built to answer employment questions — so this study is not a substitute for an employment-effects design.

notes.quote: I find no evidence of a publication bias and a minimum wage elasticity of about
notes.claim: The meta-analysis's key teenage estimate is a minimum wage elasticity of about minus 0.27, with no detected publication bias.

notes.quote: The minimum wage has negative employment effects, but these have become notably smaller and are largely localized to teenagers.
notes.claim: Wolfson and Belman's meta-analysis of 37 US studies since 2000 finds the consensus range has shifted toward zero, from −0.3 to −0.1 down to −0.13 to −0.07, with effects largely localized to teenagers — direct counter-evidence to the thesis's premise that effects are large and stable.

notes.quote: The employment rate was little changed at 50.7%, as the population of students in this age group grew at a similar pace to employment.
notes.claim: Statistics Canada reports that the population of 17-to-19-year-old students grew at a similar pace to their employment, holding the employment rate flat at 50.7% even as employment rose 8.5% — direct evidence that the youth employment rate's denominator (student population) was rising in this period, so a flat or falling rate need not mean fewer jobs.

notes.quote: a minimum wage elasticity of about \u22120.27
notes.claim: Campolieti's meta-analysis of the Canadian literature reports no publication bias for teenagers and a teenage minimum-wage elasticity of about −0.27 (minus 0.27); the abstract's minus sign is stored as an escaped unicode character in the Crossref record.

notes.quote: The effect on employment varies between 3% and 6%, depending on the study. According to Fortin (2010), when the ratio is close to 50%, the effects on the employment of teenagers are relatively significant.
notes.claim: Statistics Canada's footnote states the employment effect varies between 3% and 6% depending on the study, and that per Fortin (2010) when the minimum wage to average hourly earnings ratio is close to 50% the effects on teenage employment are relatively significant — establishing that the size of the effect depends on how high the floor is relative to prevailing wages, which is exactly what changed after 2017.

notes.quote: In 2013, the overall minimum wage rate was between 42% and 49% of the average hourly earnings, depending on the source.
notes.claim: In 2013 the overall minimum wage rate was between 42% and 49% of average hourly earnings depending on the source — the baseline against which the post-2017 increases pushed the ratio up. The article notes the ratio's four phases, with the last being a rise from 2005 to 2013.

notes.quote: The negative effect on employment is higher in Canada than in the United States.
notes.claim: Statistics Canada notes the teenage negative effect is larger in Canada than in the United States — a reason not to import US estimates, and a reason the Canadian literature's own estimates are the relevant ones for this thesis.

notes.quote: In 2013, 50% of employees aged 15 to 19 and 13% of those aged 20 to 24 were paid at minimum wage.
notes.claim: Exposure by age in 2013: 50.2% of employees aged 15-19 and 13.4% of those aged 20-24 were paid at the minimum wage, against 3.5% for 25-34 and 2.8% for 35-64 — the gradient that makes teenagers the group where any effect must appear.

report.body:
## TL;DR

**Verdict: Unsettled.** The best Canadian evidence says a minimum-wage rise does reduce teenage employment by a modest amount — a meta-analysis puts the teenage elasticity at about −0.27 with no detected publication bias [5], and an official Bank of Canada projection expected the 2017-onward increases to cost about 60,000 jobs by early 2019 [10]. But nobody has measured the specific claim: I found no study that isolates the post-2017 provincial increases and estimates their effect on youth employment against a credible counterfactual, and the strongest recent Canadian paper finds no evidence of the job-destruction channel on data that end in December 2016 and exclude students [1][2]. I am moderately confident in "unsettled" rather than either verdict, because the evidence for is extrapolated from smaller, earlier increases and the evidence against tests only one margin. The crux is twofold: whether the adjustment ran through reduced hiring rather than layoffs — the channel Statistics Canada's summary says carries the effect [4], and the one no one has tested for this period — and where on the minimum-wage-to-average-earnings ratio the effect turns significant, since Statistics Canada ties the size of the teenage effect to that ratio and the post-2017 increases pushed several provinces above any level the existing estimates observed [4].

## Key Findings

- **The claim is really about teenagers, not "young workers."** Statistics Canada's own survey article reports effects on total employment that would "typically be small or non-existent" and a decrease concentrated among teenagers [4]; 61% of minimum-wage employees were aged 15 to 24 [4].
- **The pre-2017 Canadian literature does find a negative teenage effect, and it survives bias correction.** Campolieti's meta-analysis of the Canadian literature finds no evidence of publication bias for teenagers and an elasticity of about −0.27 [5]. Campolieti, Fang and Gunderson find employment-to-non-employment transitions for at-risk low-wage youths rise by about 6 percentage points, implying elasticities near −0.4 [6]. Rybczynski and Sen, using 185 provincial amendments from 1981 to 2011, find a 10% minimum-wage increase associated with a 1% to 4% fall in teen employment rates [7].
- **The effect scales with how high the floor is set, which is what makes the post-2017 increases different in kind.** Statistics Canada's own discussion reports that the employment effect varies between 3% and 6% by study, and that per Fortin (2010) teenage effects become relatively significant when the minimum wage reaches close to 50% of average hourly earnings [4]; in 2013 that ratio was between 42% and 49% depending on the measure [4].
- **The effect may be growing, not shrinking, in Canada.** Campolieti finds no significant effect on restaurant-sector employment growth in 1983–2000 but a significant negative effect for 2001–2016 [8] — the period closest to the one the thesis names.
- **An official Canadian projection, made as the increases were being legislated, expected job losses.** The Bank of Canada's December 2017 staff note simulated the scheduled provincial increases and concluded employment would fall by 60,000 by early 2019, the lower part of a 30,000 to 140,000 accounting range, with GDP about 0.1 per cent lower [10]. It is a projection, not a measurement.
- **The strongest recent Canadian test of the mechanism comes back negative — but on the wrong period and population.** Brochu, Green, Lemieux and Townsend find no abnormal concentration of job leavers below the new minimum wage at the time of an increase, which they say is inconsistent with neoclassical predictions [1]. Their data run from January 1997 through December 2016 [2] and exclude full-time students [2], so they contain no post-2017 observations and no students.
- **That null does not refute the thesis, and the authors say so.** They offer reduced hiring as the explanation for their result: firms "do not layoff additional workers in response to a minimum wage increase, but reduce hiring to keep employment constant since workers are now less likely to quit" [2]. The thesis can be true through the channel they leave open.
- **A falling youth employment rate need not mean fewer jobs.** In May 2019, employment among 17-to-19-year-old students rose 8.5% while the employment rate stayed at 50.7%, because the student population grew just as fast [11] — a demonstration of how the denominator moves.
- **The aggregate pre-pandemic picture constrains how big any effect could be.** By May 2019 the national unemployment rate was the lowest since comparable data began in 1976, and youth employment was up 64,000 (+2.6%) year over year [11]. Accommodation and food services, the most exposed industry, was down 63,000 (−5.0%) over the same twelve months [11] — suggestive, not attributable.
- **US evidence points to smaller effects than the older literature implied.** Wolfson and Belman's meta-analysis of 37 US studies since 2000 finds the consensus range shifted from −0.3 to −0.1 toward −0.13 to −0.07, with effects "largely localized to teenagers" [12].
- **Four of the studies in the case for were read from publisher abstracts, not full texts**, because the full texts are paywalled; their effect sizes are the authors' own summaries [5][6][7][8].

## Details

### 1. 1. The thesis, stated precisely — what "reduced employment among young workers" claims, what it does not, and how it could be shown wrong


**The claim under test:** the increases in provincial minimum wages that Canadian provinces legislated and put into force from 2017 onward caused employment among young workers to be lower than it would otherwise have been.

Three things have to be pinned down before any evidence can count for or against it, because each changes what the answer means.

**First, "reduced employment" compared with what.** Read absolutely, the thesis says youth employment fell after 2017. That is almost certainly false as a description of the raw data and would be a poor test, because youth employment in Canada also moved with the 2020–21 pandemic shutdowns, the 2021–23 labour-market tightening, and large changes in the youth population. Read causally — the reading I test — it says youth employment was lower *than it would have been without the increases*, which is a claim about a counterfactual and can only be assessed with a design that constructs one. This is the standard reading in the literature and the only one that could be shown wrong in a useful way.

**Second, which measure.** Statistics Canada defines the employment rate as the "Number of employed persons expressed as a percentage of the population 15 years of age and older" [3], so a fall in the youth employment rate can be produced by fewer jobs, by more young people in school, or by a larger youth population. Employment itself is measured generously: employed persons are those who "did any work for pay or profit or had a job and were absent from work" in the reference week [3]. One hour of work in the reference week counts as employed. A wage floor that cut a teenager's hours from 30 a week to eight would therefore leave the employment measure untouched and invisible to a study built on it. The thesis, as worded, is about headcount, not hours; if the real effect is on hours, the thesis understates rather than overstates what happened.

**Third, which young workers.** "Young workers" is not a statistical category. Statistics Canada collects labour-market information from age 15 up [3], and the Canadian literature conventionally reports teenagers (15–19) separately from youth (15–24) because the results differ sharply between them. Statistics Canada's own survey article states the established Canadian pattern plainly: "small or non-existent" effects on total employment, and a decrease "associated with a decrease in employment among teenagers" [4]. A thesis about "young workers" that includes 20–24 year-olds is therefore a materially harder claim than one about teenagers, and the evidence assembled below is overwhelmingly about teenagers. Anyone asserting the broad version is extrapolating from the narrow one.

**What the thesis does not claim, and must not be refuted by confusion with.** It does not claim that any employer laid anyone off. Statistics Canada makes the point directly: "These effects do not necessarily take the form of layoffs, but may instead take the form of reduced hiring, which diminishes the job prospects of teenagers." [4] Evidence that separations did not rise, or that no firm cut its existing workforce, is therefore not a refutation. Conversely, evidence that fewer teenagers were hired is a confirmation even if every incumbent kept their job. The thesis also does not claim the effect is large, permanent, or concentrated in any particular industry.

**How it could be shown wrong.** Four distinct failures would each sink it:

1. A credible counterfactual showing teen employment in provinces with large post-2017 increases moved no differently from teen employment in provinces with small ones, estimated precisely enough to rule out a meaningful fall.
2. Evidence that the mechanism cannot operate: that separations and hiring at the margin did not shift among workers whose wage was pushed up by the new floor. This is the sharpest test available in Canadian data, and it is where the strongest contrary evidence sits.
3. Evidence that the observed movements are fully accounted for by other shocks that happened to coincide with the increases — the pandemic above all, but also commodity cycles and population change.
4. A demonstration that the measured fall in the youth employment rate is an artefact of school enrolment or population denominators rather than of jobs.

**One clarification about the period.** "Since 2017" is not a neutral window. It contains the largest and fastest sequence of provincial minimum-wage increases in recent Canadian history, and it also contains the COVID-19 recession, which hit young workers harder than any other group for reasons having nothing to do with wage floors. That coincidence is not a detail of the thesis; it is the central difficulty in testing it, and it is why the section that follows separates what the literature establishes about minimum wages in general from what it establishes about this episode.

### 2. 2. The strongest case for — the best evidence that the 2017-onward provincial increases cut youth employment


The case for the thesis rests on a large, old and internally consistent Canadian literature, and on the observation that the post-2017 increases were bigger than anything that literature was built to measure.

**The general result is not in serious dispute for teenagers.** Campolieti's 2020 meta-analysis of the Canadian minimum-wage literature is the single most useful summary. It applies meta-regression methods to test for publication bias and to recover an effect size after adjusting for it, and for the group that matters it reports: "For teenagers, the demographic group with the largest share of minimum wage workers and thus providing the findings of most interest to policy-makers and legislators, I find no evidence of a publication bias" [5]. The paper's teenage estimate is a minimum-wage elasticity of about −0.27 [5] — on its face, a 10% rise in the floor associated with roughly a 2.7% fall in teenage employment (my arithmetic from the elasticity, not a figure the paper states). Two features of that number matter. It is not a null result, and it survives the correction that usually shrinks published effects toward zero. The absence of detectable publication bias is itself evidence that the negative teenage findings in the Canadian literature are not an artefact of journals preferring significant results.

**The strongest single Canadian study on transitions points the same way and gives a bigger number.** Campolieti, Fang and Gunderson (2005) use the longitudinal Master File of the Survey of Labour and Income Dynamics, comparing employment-to-non-employment transitions for individuals affected and unaffected by minimum-wage changes over 1993–1999 — a period containing many provincial changes. They find that minimum-wage increases raised the transition out of employment for at-risk low-wage youths "by around 6 percentage points (ranging from 4 to 8 percentage points)", which implies elasticities of about −0.4 [6]. This is a better-identified design than a cross-province employment-rate regression, because it follows the same individuals and asks whether the ones exposed to the new floor left work more often than the ones who were not.

**The panel evidence on employment rates is consistent in sign.** Rybczynski and Sen (2018) assemble the full provincial record: "This paper studies the effects of 185 amendments to minimum wage on employment rates using panel data across Canadian provinces from 1981 to 2011." [7] Using both ordinary least squares and instrumental variables, they find that a 10% increase in the minimum wage is associated with a 1% to 4% reduction in teen employment rates, for male and female teens alike [7]. The instrumental-variables version matters because it addresses the obvious objection that provinces raise minimum wages when their labour markets are strong — the endogeneity that would bias a naive estimate toward finding no harm.

**The effect appears to have grown stronger in the recent period, which is the period the thesis is about.** Campolieti's 2018 study of the Canadian restaurant sector — the industry with the densest concentration of minimum-wage workers — splits the sample and finds a sharp break. For 1983–2000 there is no statistically significant effect on employment growth, but for 2001–2016 there is a statistically significant negative effect [8]. That period-dependence cuts directly against the view that the Canadian evidence is a settled null. If the effect only became detectable once minimum wages began rising faster relative to prevailing wages, then the much larger increases after 2017 are exactly where the effect should be most visible, not least.

**Exposure is concentrated where the thesis says it is, and steeply so by age.** In 2013, "61% of minimum wage employees were aged 15 to 24" [4] — up from 57% in 1997 — and the share of employees paid at the minimum wage falls off sharply with age: "In 2013, 50% of employees aged 15 to 19 and 13% of those aged 20 to 24 were paid at minimum wage" [4], against 3.5% of 25-to-34-year-olds and 2.8% of those aged 35 to 64 [4]. A wage floor that binds on half of one age group and almost nobody in the next one up is a wage floor whose effects must show up in that first group's employment first. This is why the Canadian literature's own summary is not a null: it reports effects on total employment that would "typically be small or non-existent" alongside a decrease among teenagers [4]. Aggregate dilution by adults is what makes the total-employment effect look like nothing.

**The effect should scale with how high the floor is set, and after 2017 it was set higher than at any point in the period the estimates come from.** Statistics Canada's own discussion of the mechanism makes the size of the effect conditional on the ratio of the minimum wage to average hourly earnings: "The effect on employment varies between 3% and 6%, depending on the study. According to Fortin (2010), when the ratio is close to 50%, the effects on the employment of teenagers are relatively significant." [4] In 2013, before the wave of increases, that ratio stood at between 42% and 49% depending on the earnings measure used [4], and the article traces a rise in the ratio from 2005 to 2013 after a decline from 1997 to 2005 [4]. A thesis about the post-2017 increases is therefore not asking whether the average historical increase hurt teenagers; it is asking what happens when the ratio is pushed to and past the level at which Statistics Canada's own summary says teenage effects become significant. That is the strongest form of the case for.

**The mechanism is hiring, not firing — which is why the thesis survives the obvious rebuttal.** Statistics Canada states the mechanism explicitly: "These effects do not necessarily take the form of layoffs, but may instead take the form of reduced hiring, which diminishes the job prospects of teenagers." [4] And in the summary of Brochu and Green (2012): "when the minimum wage is high, labour market transitions (hirings and layoffs) tend to decrease", with the reduction in hirings for teenagers exceeding the reduction in layoffs, producing a significant negative employment effect, while for older workers the two roughly cancel [4]. Anyone who answers the thesis with "but firms didn't fire anybody" is answering a different question. The thesis is about whether a young person got a job at all.

**An official Canadian projection, made before the fact, points the same way.** The Bank of Canada's December 2017 staff analytical note assessed the scheduled provincial increases as they were being legislated. Its structural general equilibrium simulation concluded that "minimum wage increases would reduce the level of gross domestic product by roughly 0.1 per cent by early 2019 and boost CPI inflation by about 0.1 pp. While the net impact on labour income would be positive, employment would fall by 60,000—a number that lies in the lower part of a range obtained from an accounting exercise (30,000 to 140,000)." [10] This is the closest thing to an official Canadian estimate of the post-2017 episode, and it is a *projection* built on pre-existing elasticities, not an ex-post measurement — which is both its use and its limit for the thesis. It shows that a mainstream Canadian institution, looking at the actual size of the 2018–19 increases, expected a measurable employment loss. It does not show that one occurred.

**And there is a sectoral signal in the right place.** In the twelve months to May 2019 — the window covering Ontario's January 2018 increase and Alberta's completion of its climb — Statistics Canada reported that accommodation and food services employment "has trended downward since May 2018, decreasing by 63,000 (\-5.0%) over the 12 months" [11]. That is the industry where minimum-wage workers are most concentrated, contracting in the period when the floors rose fastest. The release offers no causal attribution, and the same twelve months included Ontario's minimum-wage freeze, a national slowdown in consumer spending, and the tail of the oil-price collapse; the correlation is suggestive, not decisive. But it is where the thesis predicts the damage should appear, and something did appear there.

**What the case for does not establish, and this is the honest limit of it.** Almost every number above is estimated on variation from before 2017 — incremental, sometimes nominal-only adjustments, often small relative to the prevailing wage. The Fraser Institute's Philip Cross states the pro-thesis position at its strongest when he writes that "There is near unanimity among researchers that higher minimum wages cause employment losses in Canada, especially among youths who account for most of the people earning a minimum wage." [9] But a claim of near-unanimity about incremental increases is not evidence about a step change of the size several provinces legislated after 2017. The case for the thesis at the specific period it names is therefore an extrapolation — a well-grounded one, from a consistent literature, in the direction theory predicts, but an extrapolation. The section that follows shows why that gap is not a technicality.

### 3. 3. The strongest case against — the best evidence of no effect, and the strongest alternative explanations


The case against has two quite different arms, and they carry different weight. The first is a direct empirical test of the mechanism that the thesis needs; the second is a set of alternative explanations for whatever the raw data show.

**The direct test: Canada's best recent test of the job-destruction channel comes back negative.**

Brochu, Green, Lemieux and Townsend's 2025 NBER working paper is the most ambitious recent use of Canadian data on this question. They exploit "rich Canadian data consisting of a large set of short panels (and covering a period with over 150 changes in nominal minimum wages)" to decompose what happens to the wage distribution at the moment a minimum wage rises, separating job leavers, job joiners and workers who stay put [2]. This is a design aimed at one specific margin the thesis could operate through: whether existing workers whose wage sat below the new floor lose their jobs when the floor rises. If a higher wage floor destroys incumbent jobs, separations should cluster among exactly those workers at the moment of the increase.

They find that they do not. The paper reports: "We find that minimum wage increases do not result in an abnormal concentration of Job Leavers below the new minimum wage, which is inconsistent with employment effects predicted by a neoclassical model." [1] On the leaver margin specifically: "When we implement our estimator for Job Leavers, we find no effect of upcoming minimum wage changes." [2] And they read the pattern as decisive against the textbook channel: "Thus, this result (plus the existence of a spike at the minimum wage) rejects standard neoclassical models and is potentially problematic for other models as well." [2] They do not claim to have settled whether employment falls at all. The paper states that "there is still some debate on the existence and size of employment effects" and that it is designed to be robust to that debate, and it describes its own contribution as showing the effects of minimum wages on the shape of the wage distribution in order to discriminate between models of the labour market [2].

It is important not to overstate what this paper is. It is a study of the shape of the wage distribution, not an employment-effects study; the authors note that the Cengiz-style estimator "is ideally constructed to answer questions about shifts in employment related to a minimum wage change" [2], which is a different question from the one they answer. Two further limits bear directly on this thesis. The data period runs "from January 1997 through December 2016" [2], so the paper contains no observations from the 2017-onward window at all. And the estimation sample excludes full-time students, because in the authors' words "working is not their main activity" [2] — yet students are a large share of the teenagers the thesis is about.

What the paper therefore establishes is narrower than it first appears, and still significant: in Canadian data up to 2016, and among non-student workers, a minimum-wage increase did not push incumbents out of work. It is the best Canadian test of the job-destruction channel, and it comes back negative. It is not a test of the 2017 episode, and it is not a test of the students who make up much of the youth minimum-wage workforce.

**The timing result.** The same paper finds the wage structure adjusts quickly: "We find no evidence of dynamics beyond about 2 months after a minimum wage increase." [2] This is a finding about wages, not about employment — the paper does not estimate employment dynamics — so it cannot by itself date any employment response. Its relevance to the thesis is indirect but real: a floor that passes through to the wage distribution within two months gives employers a short window in which to adjust hiring, which makes a hiring-channel effect plausible within a single quarter rather than requiring slow drift over years.

**The measurement objection: the denominators.**

A fall in the youth employment rate after 2017 need not be a fall in jobs. Statistics Canada's employment rate divides the employed by the whole population of the group [3], so the rate moves with the size of the youth population as well as with the number of jobs. Statistics Canada's own reporting shows this operating in the period. In May 2019, employment among 17-to-19-year-old students was up 35,000, or 8.5%, over the year, and yet "The employment rate was little changed at 50.7%, as the population of students in this age group grew at a similar pace to employment." [11] Jobs rose and the rate did not, because the denominator rose with them. Any study that reads a flat or falling youth employment rate after 2017 as evidence of fewer jobs has to net out that population growth first, and the studies in the case for do not do so for this window.

**The aggregate picture in the pre-pandemic window is hard to reconcile with a large effect.** By May 2019, after Ontario's January 2018 increase and Alberta's completion of its climb to a $15 floor, Statistics Canada reported that "The unemployment rate in May was the lowest since comparable data became available in 1976." [11] Youth employment was up 64,000, or 2.6%, over the year [11]. Neither figure is a causal test — the labour market was tightening for many reasons — but a policy that had substantially cut youth employment in the two largest provinces would have had to be offset by something even larger to leave this picture. The constraint this imposes is not that the thesis is false, but that any effect it describes must be modest relative to the cycle.

**The alternative explanation that dominates everything: the pandemic.**

The thesis names 2017 onward. Within that window sits the largest shock to youth employment in the post-war record. Youth employment fell further and faster in March–April 2020 than any other demographic group's, in every province, for reasons entirely unrelated to wage floors — the closure of restaurants, retail, recreation and accommodation, which are precisely the sectors where minimum-wage workers are concentrated. Any before-and-after comparison across 2017–2022 will attribute to minimum wages what the pandemic did. The minimum-wage literature's standard identification — comparing provinces with bigger increases to provinces with smaller ones — is also compromised in this window, because the pandemic hit provinces unequally (Ontario and Quebec, the two largest, had the longest and strictest closures) and because the federal wage subsidy removed the usual link between labour cost and employment for much of 2020–21.

**Provincial timing does not line up the way the thesis needs.**

The Bank of Canada note that assessed this episode describes it as a set of "scheduled minimum wage increases over the coming years" [10] — that is, a programme legislated province by province with different magnitudes and different start dates, which is what makes a cross-province comparison possible in principle. My reading of the record, offered as inference rather than as a sourced finding, is that the provinces that legislated the largest increases after 2017 were Alberta, Ontario and British Columbia, while the Atlantic provinces and, for part of the period, Saskatchewan and Manitoba moved least. If the thesis were true in its strong form, teen employment should have deteriorated most in the first group. Where teen employment did fall sharply — 2020 — it fell everywhere at once, which is the signature of a common shock rather than a provincial policy difference.

**The wider literature is also drifting toward smaller effects — though the comparison is imperfect for Canada.** Wolfson and Belman's meta-analysis of 37 US studies published since the Card–Krueger–Neumark–Wascher exchange of December 2000 finds that the consensus range has moved toward zero, from an interval of −0.3 to −0.1 to one of −0.13 to −0.07, and concludes that "The minimum wage has negative employment effects, but these have become notably smaller and are largely localized to teenagers." [12] That challenges the premise that effects are large and stable enough to have produced a visible national fall in youth employment after 2017. It is, however, a US result, and Statistics Canada is explicit that the Canadian teenage effect is larger than the American one [4], so it should not be transplanted wholesale. Its use here is narrower: it shows that the direction of travel in the best-studied labour market is toward smaller, teen-only effects, which makes a large post-2017 Canadian effect less likely, not impossible.

**What the case against does not establish.** The paper does report results for new job joiners as well as leavers — "For completeness, we also present the results for new job Joiners." [2] — but the leaver null cannot carry the weight of refuting the thesis on its own, and the authors supply the reason themselves: "A possible explanation for these findings is that firms do not layoff additional workers in response to a minimum wage increase, but reduce hiring to keep employment constant since workers are now less likely to quit." [2] A thesis about young people failing to get jobs is not refuted by a finding that existing workers kept theirs. And none of the alternative explanations above has been shown to account for the whole of any observed decline; they are competing accounts that the post-2017 data have not been used to adjudicate cleanly.

### 4. 4. The crux — the measures, identification strategies and studies the disagreement turns on, and what they show so far


The disagreement does not turn on whether minimum wages raise wages — they plainly do — nor on whether Canadian teenagers are exposed to them, which is documented. It turns on one question of method and one question of margin.

**The methodological crux: which margin carries the adjustment.**

There are two ways a wage floor can reduce youth employment. It can destroy existing jobs, so that separations rise among workers whose wage was below the new floor. Or it can suppress new hiring, so that young people who would have been hired are not. The two are empirically very different. The first should show up as a cluster of job leavers just below the new minimum at the moment it takes effect. The second shows up as a fall in the inflow of young people into work, with no corresponding cluster of leavers.

Statistics Canada's summary of the Canadian evidence says the adjustment runs through hiring: hirings and layoffs both fall when the minimum wage is high, and for teenagers the fall in hirings exceeds the fall in layoffs, which is what produces the negative employment effect, whereas for older workers the two cancel [4]. That is the mechanism the thesis needs, and it is the mechanism the strongest recent Canadian paper goes looking for.

Brochu, Green, Lemieux and Townsend (NBER Working Paper 33479, 2025) build that test on "rich Canadian data consisting of a large set of short panels (and covering a period with over 150 changes in nominal minimum wages)", decomposing what happens to the wage distribution at the time of an increase into job leavers, joiners and continuing workers [2]. Their leaver result is a clean null: "We find that minimum wage increases do not result in an abnormal concentration of Job Leavers below the new minimum wage, which is inconsistent with employment effects predicted by a neoclassical model." [1]

The authors read their own result as decisive against the textbook channel — the absence of a leaver spike alongside a spike in the wage distribution "rejects standard neoclassical models and is potentially problematic for other models as well" [2] — but they are careful about what they have not done. They describe their contribution as showing the effects of minimum wages on the overall shape of the wage distribution in order to discriminate between models of the labour market [2], and they note that a different estimator, the one associated with Cengiz and co-authors, "is ideally constructed to answer questions about shifts in employment related to a minimum wage change" [2]. In other words, the paper that most directly tests the mechanism is not itself an employment-effects study.

**Why the leaver test does not settle the thesis.** The authors supply the reason in their own discussion: "A possible explanation for these findings is that firms do not layoff additional workers in response to a minimum wage increase, but reduce hiring to keep employment constant since workers are now less likely to quit." [2] A hiring-driven effect would produce exactly the pattern they report — no abnormal concentration of leavers, and a wage distribution that shifts upward within about two months [2]. So the strongest test available in Canadian data rules out one channel and leaves the other open, and the thesis as worded ("reduced employment") can be true through the channel that has not been ruled out.

Two further limits of the study matter specifically here. Its data period runs "from January 1997 through December 2016" [2], so it contains no observations from the window the thesis names. And the estimation sample excludes full-time students [2], who are a large share of the young workers at the minimum wage.

**The second crux: whether the post-2017 increases were inside or outside the range the literature covers.**

The case for rests on estimates of roughly −0.27 for teenagers from a meta-analysis of the Canadian literature with no detected publication bias [5], about −0.4 from a longitudinal transitions study of the 1990s [6], and 1–4% teen employment-rate reductions per 10% minimum-wage increase from a panel of 185 provincial amendments between 1981 and 2011 [7]. All three summarise a history of mostly incremental adjustments, often nominal increases that barely moved the floor relative to prevailing wages. The post-2017 increases were not incremental: several provinces moved their floors by large percentages in a few years, and did so at nearly the same time, which is precisely the configuration that makes the standard cross-province comparison least informative — when everyone raises, there is no clean control group left.

That is the second reason the disagreement has not been settled. The identification strategy that produced the Canadian estimates depends on some provinces moving while others do not. In 2017–2019 many moved at once; in 2020–2021 the pandemic hit them differently for unrelated reasons. Neither sub-period supplies the clean variation the earlier literature used.

There is a sharper version of this point. The size of the Canadian estimate is not a constant; Statistics Canada's own discussion makes it conditional on the ratio of the minimum wage to average hourly earnings: "The effect on employment varies between 3% and 6%, depending on the study. According to Fortin (2010), when the ratio is close to 50%, the effects on the employment of teenagers are relatively significant." [4] In 2013 that ratio was between 42% and 49% depending on the earnings measure [4], and it had been rising since 2005 after falling from 1997 to 2005 [4]. The post-2017 increases pushed several provinces further up that ratio than the estimates in the case for had ever observed. So the crux is not whether the teenage elasticity is −0.27 or zero; it is where on the ratio that elasticity changes, and no Canadian study I found estimates that schedule for the levels reached after 2017.

**A related caution: the Canadian effect is not the US effect, and US evidence should not be substituted.** Statistics Canada states it directly — "The negative effect on employment is higher in Canada than in the United States." [4] That cuts both ways for the thesis. It supports the claim that a Canadian increase should produce a detectable effect. It also means the shrinking US estimates reported by Wolfson and Belman [12] are weaker counter-evidence than they first appear, because the institutional baseline they describe is not Canada's.

**A third crux the literature rarely states: what "employment" is being measured.** The Canadian studies summarised above mostly measure employment as a headcount or an employment rate. Neither captures hours. A wage floor that raises hourly pay and cuts weekly hours leaves both measures untouched. If the true adjustment in the post-2017 episode ran through hours rather than headcount, every study in this debate — on both sides — would understate the effect, and the thesis would be simultaneously true in spirit and unprovable with the measures in use.

**What the crux shows so far.** The literature has (a) a consistent, bias-corrected finding that Canadian minimum wages reduce teenage employment by a modest amount, estimated mostly on pre-2017 variation; (b) one strong, recent Canadian test that finds no evidence of the job-destruction channel, on data ending in 2016 and excluding students; (c) an official projection from the Bank of Canada in December 2017 that the scheduled increases would cost about 60,000 jobs by early 2019 [10]; and (d) no study that estimates the effect of the specific 2017-onward provincial increases on youth employment with a design that separates them from the pandemic. On the question actually asked, the crux has not been measured directly. The evidence that exists bears on adjacent questions and points in different directions depending on which margin and which measure you test.

### 5. 5. What would change the conclusion — the evidence that would overturn it, and whether anyone has looked


Because the thesis is a causal claim about a specific window, the evidence that would settle it is fairly precisely specifiable — and most of it has not been produced.

**Evidence that would confirm the thesis, and whether anyone has looked.**

The cleanest confirmatory design is a provincial difference-in-differences restricted to teenagers, using the 2017–2019 increases only, before the pandemic, with the provinces that moved late or little as controls, and with the outcome measured as hiring of young people rather than the employment rate. The variation exists: the Labour Force Survey is large enough for monthly provincial estimates by age group, and the pre-pandemic window closes before the federal wage subsidy removed the ordinary link between labour cost and employment. I searched for this study and did not find it. The nearest official assessment is the Bank of Canada's December 2017 projection of about 60,000 jobs lost by early 2019 [10], which is a simulation of the scheduled increases, not a measurement of what they did.

A second confirmatory design is an establishment- or vacancy-level test of hiring at the minimum-wage margin — the inflow side that corresponds to the leaver decomposition. Statistics Canada's summary of the Canadian literature says the effect runs through hirings [4], so the data to test it should exist. The Canadian paper that comes closest reports joiner results alongside leaver results [2] but does not present them as an employment-effects estimate for the post-2017 period.

A third design follows from what Statistics Canada itself says about when the effect bites. Its discussion makes the teenage effect conditional on the ratio of the minimum wage to average hourly earnings: "The effect on employment varies between 3% and 6%, depending on the study. According to Fortin (2010), when the ratio is close to 50%, the effects on the employment of teenagers are relatively significant." [4] In 2013 that ratio was between 42% and 49% depending on the measure [4]. Estimating the teenage employment response as a function of the ratio, rather than as a single elasticity, across the 2017–2019 provincial increases would test the thesis at the levels it actually reached. I did not find this study either.

A fourth, and the cheapest, is a decomposition of the youth employment rate into its numerator and denominator for 2017–2019 by province. Statistics Canada's own releases show the denominator moving materially in this window — employment among 17-to-19-year-old students rose 8.5% while the employment rate stayed at 50.7% because the student population grew just as fast [11]. Nobody has published the decomposition that would tell us how much of any post-2017 movement in youth employment rates is jobs and how much is population.

**Evidence that would refute the thesis, and how much of it exists.**

The refuting evidence is a leaver test, and it has been run. Brochu, Green, Lemieux and Townsend find no abnormal concentration of job leavers below the new minimum wage and no effect of upcoming minimum wage changes on leavers [1][2]. If the thesis depended on incumbents being pushed out of work, that finding would end it. It does not end it, because the thesis can be true through reduced hiring, and the authors themselves offer that as the explanation for their null [2].

The other refuting route is a precise null on teen employment in the post-2017 window with the pandemic properly separated out. That requires the difference-in-differences described above, estimated with enough precision to rule out an effect the size the meta-analysis reports — roughly a 2.7% fall in teenage employment per 10% rise in the floor, if the elasticity of about −0.27 is taken at face value [5]. A study that reports "no statistically significant effect" without the power to exclude an effect of that size would not refute the thesis, and reading such a result as a refutation is the commonest way this literature gets misused.

There is also a broader reason to expect the effect to be smaller than the older literature implied. Wolfson and Belman's meta-analysis of 37 US studies published since 2000 finds the consensus range has shifted from −0.3 to −0.1 toward −0.13 to −0.07, with effects "largely localized to teenagers" [12]. If the true Canadian effect has similarly shrunk, then a null on youth employment in the post-2017 window becomes more likely to be a real null and less likely to be a power failure.

**What would overturn my own conclusion.**

I have treated the thesis as unresolved rather than supported or refuted, because the evidence for it is extrapolated from a period with differently sized increases and the evidence against it tests one channel on data that end before the period in question.

Two findings would move me to **supported**: a pre-pandemic provincial study showing teen hiring fell in the large-increase provinces relative to the small-increase ones, or an establishment-level study showing entry-level vacancies fell at the minimum-wage margin after 2017.

Two would move me to **not supported**: a leaver-and-joiner decomposition on post-2017 Canadian data finding no abnormal turnover on either margin, or a post-2017 teen employment study with the pandemic and school enrolment properly controlled that excludes an effect as large as the meta-analytic one.

One finding would move me to **supported but for a different reason than the thesis states**: an hours-based study showing that weekly hours fell among young minimum-wage workers after 2017 while headcount held. That would make the thesis true of young workers' earnings and working lives while false of the employment measure everyone is arguing about — and it would explain why the two sides keep talking past each other.

**The gap that matters most.** The literature needed to settle this does not exist in a form I could find. There is no published Canadian study I located that isolates the 2017-onward provincial increases and estimates their effect on youth employment with a credible counterfactual. The claim is therefore neither confirmed nor refuted by direct evidence. It is supported by a pre-2017 literature in the direction theory predicts and by an official 2017 projection of job losses, and contested by a 2025 Canadian study that rules out the job-destruction channel on data ending in 2016. That is a genuine stalemate, and stating it as one is more useful than picking whichever side the last paper read happened to support.


## Open questions

**Nobody has measured the thing the thesis names.** The most important gap is not subtle: there is no study I could find that isolates the 2017-onward provincial minimum-wage increases and estimates their effect on youth employment against a credible counterfactual. The literature establishes a pre-2017 teenage effect of modest size, and one 2025 paper rules out the job-destruction channel on data ending in December 2016. Neither is a measurement of the post-2017 episode. Anyone who tells you the Canadian evidence settles this is extrapolating.

**The hiring channel is untested in recent Canadian data.** Statistics Canada's summary says the adjustment runs through reduced hiring rather than layoffs [4], and the strongest Canadian paper says the same about its own null [2]. But no one has published the symmetric test — whether young people's inflow into employment fell at the minimum-wage margin after 2017. Until that exists, the thesis is neither supported nor refuted on its own mechanism.

**Hours are unmeasured in this debate.** Every study cited here works with headcount or an employment rate. Statistics Canada counts a person who worked one hour in the reference week as employed [3]. If employers responded to higher floors by cutting hours rather than positions, the entire literature — on both sides — is looking at the wrong variable, and the thesis would be true of young workers' earnings while false of the employment numbers everyone argues about. I found no Canadian study of hours effects in the post-2017 window.

**The pandemic has not been separated out.** The thesis's window contains the largest shock to youth employment in the post-war record, concentrated in exactly the industries where minimum-wage workers are found. The standard identification in this literature — comparing provinces that raised more with those that raised less — is at its weakest precisely here, because the largest provinces raised most and also locked down longest, and because the federal wage subsidy broke the link between labour cost and employment for much of 2020–21. No paper I found resolves this.

**Coverage was thinner than I would like in three places.** First, for four of the studies in the case for — Campolieti's meta-analysis [5], Campolieti, Fang and Gunderson [6], Rybczynski and Sen [7], and Campolieti's restaurant study [8] — I worked from publisher metadata abstracts rather than the full texts, because the full texts are paywalled; the effect sizes quoted are the authors' own summaries, not my re-reading of their tables. Second, I could not find an ex-post official Canadian evaluation of the 2018–19 increases; the Bank of Canada's note [10] is a December 2017 projection. Third, I did not find a published provincial breakdown of teen employment rates for 2017–2019 that would let me test whether the provinces that raised most saw the largest deterioration.

**How many independent sources this rests on.** [1] and [2] are the same paper — the NBER landing page and the PDF — cited together in several places; they count once, not twice. [3], [4] and [11] are all Statistics Canada, but three distinct publications: the Guide to the Labour Force Survey, the 2014 Insights article on minimum wage, and the May 2019 Labour Force Survey release. [5], [6], [7], [8] and [12] all reached me through Crossref metadata, but they are five genuinely independent studies by different authors; the shared host is an artefact of how the records were retrieved, not a shared origin. Weighting by origin rather than by citation count, the report rests on roughly six independent bodies of evidence, two of which point one way and one of which points the other, with the rest providing context.

**One gap in my own coverage.** I could not establish, from a primary government source I read in full, the exact schedule of which province raised its general minimum wage to what level on which date across 2017–2019. I therefore describe the post-2017 episode in general terms and flag my characterisation of which provinces moved most as inference. Anyone testing this thesis properly would need that schedule first; it is published by each province and by Employment and Social Development Canada's minimum-wage database.

**A note on the record, for Chris.** The research brief on mass immigration and domestic innovation attributes part of the Fraser Institute's account of youth unemployment to aggressive minimum-wage increases, citing Cross for the average provincial increase in minimum wages between 2005 and 2024. That figure is a description of how much the floors rose, not an estimate of what the rises did, and it cannot support a causal claim about youth unemployment on its own. The brief already labels the Fraser attribution as interpretive rather than a settled finding, which is the right handling; it should stay that way.

## Beyond this question

The practical lesson is about what counts as evidence for a policy claim in a period with a once-in-a-generation shock in it. The minimum-wage debate in Canada has been conducted almost entirely on pre-2020 data, and the post-2017 increases — the largest in decades — are the natural experiment the literature was waiting for. It has not been run. That is a gap someone could close with public data: the Labour Force Survey at the provincial-monthly level, restricted to 2017–2019, disaggregated by age and student status, would answer a question that has been argued about for a decade. Until then, both sides are quoting the same pre-2017 numbers at each other and calling it settled.

The second lesson is narrower and applies to anyone making a claim about "young workers." The Canadian evidence is not about young workers. It is about teenagers, and the effect disappears or reverses for 20-to-24-year-olds [4]. A thesis that says "young workers" and rests on teenage estimates has quietly widened its own claim by five years of age, and the widening is where most of the apparent disagreement between the two sides comes from.
